The following item appeared in the Ottawa ' Citizen ' of yesterday which I think is worthy of consideration, and as to which I wish to ask for some information :

The work of demolishing the buildings on Sussex street where the new departmental block is to be located is progressing. It was stated at the Department of Public Works today that the new plans are practically finished and at present the specifications are in course of preparation. It is intended to call for bids within a few weeks or in good time to allow for the commencement of operations in the spring. A substantial vote for the purpose appears in the main estimates. The plan has been altered materially through a story being taken off the building, while it has also been made narrower. The tower and top ornamentation has also been changed. The total cost will likely be about three and a half millions and big contractors from all over the Dominion have been making inquiries with a view of submitting tenders.
This indicates most important alterations in the new plans for the new departmental buildings. I do not profess to have any particular knowledge on a question of this kind, but I think we all look upon these public buildings in Ottawa as a national asset, and desire to see them worthy of this great Dominion. We aro very proud of the buildings in which we sit at the present moment ; they constitute a beautiful block, and are well worthy their position as the seat of legislation for this Dominion. But, since the days in which these buildings were erected it appears to me there has been a gradual deterioration. The Langevin block is a dignified structure although it is not in harmony with the other buildings on these grounds, but from the parliamentary block down to the mint, and the archives buildings there is a very great descent indeed. The archives building with its cardboard battlements, and its altogether flimsy appearance is in no way worthy of the Dominion. Even the Victoria 'ipuseum, although it has considerable dignity on account of its size, appears to lack many details which might have been supplied had competent expert architects passed upon the designs. I consider that the architects of the present day, generally speaking, are on just as high a level as those of the past, and we have a pretty good example of modern architecture in the splendid building which is being erected by the Grand Trunk Railway Company in Ottawa. I cannot help but think that with a proper effort the new departmental buildings could be made just as well suited to occupy the position they will hold in the Capital of the Dominion, as are the parliamentary buildings. Some years ago when this question was first brought up the House understood that following the precedent adopted elsewhere a competition was to be held for the purpose of obtaining the best designs possible from architects all over the world, but the prizes offered were hardly large enough to bring out the very best efforts of able architects. A year or two ago when the Lon-

don county council purposed erecting new buildings they offered an enormous prize, and I understand the designs submitted provide for buildings quite worthy of the purposes for which they are intended. What has been done in connection with this competition? Have the prizes been awarded, and is the successful competitor to be entrusted with the new building?

Prizes were awarded by the committee entrusted with the consideration of the plans and awarding of prizes, but the department did not decide to accept any of the plans, and plans have been prepared by the architectural staff of the department under the direction of the chief architect.
Are these designs to be submitted to a body of experts before tenders are called for, as indicated by this article?
No, except to the experts of the department.

This is a most important matter, and it is due to this House and this country that some more inspection should be made of these plans than apparently is proposed by the Minister of Public Works. However good, and however able his architects may be, I do not think it is sufficient simply to put this matter into the hands of one body of men, wo ought to have these plans on exhibition, so that the public at large may see them, may *criticise them and a body of experts should be appointed to look into them. The members should also have an opportunity of seeing the plans and understanding the nature of the building for which they are asked to appropriate this enormous sum of money. As I said, it seems to me, that the last buildings constructed in this city entirely from the designs of the department are not of such a character as in my humble judgment the great public departmental buildings of the Capital of Canada should be.

As I have explained, some years ago, before I became minister, competitive designs were invited from Canadian architects. A number of designs were submitted and the committee of architects to whom the plans were referred, decided upon three sets of plans to which the first, second and third prizes were awarded. The plans were all exhibited in the Railway Committee room. After careful consideration, the department decided to adopt none of these plans for reasons which seemed good to the department.
Was that on the question of style or of cost ?

On the question of style of the plans. In the opinion of the department, and I and other members of
the government who saw the plans, entertained the same view, none of these plans were the best that could be devised and it was decided to direct the chief architect to prepare new plans. These plans were exhibited last session.
My hon. friend has referred to an article in the ' Citizen ' about an alteration in the plans. An alteration has been made, and I regretted this, but it was necessary, in view of certain improvements in the nature of a driveway by the Ottawa Improvement Commission. Owing to this driveway it was thought better to preserve Mackenzie avenue as a public highway. In the previous plans, a building was provided to encroach upon or entirely take up Mackenzie avenue. Upon consideration and after hearing the views of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, the government decided that it would be better to leave Mackenzie avenue open as a public highway, as a part of the driveway. That necessitated narrowing the building. Then came the question whether we should leave the building of the same height. It will be understood that in erecting a departmental building of that size, it was desirable to have a well in the centre to afford light to the inner offices.
What is the width from Mackenzie avenue to Sussex street ?

About 200 feet. As we had to narrow the building by about 40 feet in order to leave Mackenzie avenue vacant, it became necessary, in order to give sufficient light to the offices on the well, to reduce the height of the buildings by at least one story. This will greatly improve the building so far as the lighting of the inner offices is concerned. The original plan provided for 7. stories on Sussex street and 6 on Mackenzie avenue. Under the changed plans there will be 6 stories on Sussex street and 5 on Mackenzie avenue.
A word in regard to the architecture of the buildings recently erected by the government. I do not profess to be any more skilled in architecture than by hon. friend, but I think I can safely say that opinions differ very much if my hon. friend's opinion reflects the views of any considerable number of people, because I have heard a good many people speak in terms of high praise of the Archives Building, of the Mint, and more especially of the Victoria Memorial Museum, which is spoken of as being of very beautiful design and one of which the country may well feel proud. My hon. friend speaks of the Grand Trunk hotel, which I think is a very fine building. But I am sure that if it were a public building if would receive a lot of criticism. Many people would say that there is not sufficient ornamentation about it, that it is too plain, and altogether unattractive, and yet

it is a very fine building. I can point my hon. friend to many buildings around the city which are being erected by private individuals under architects of skill and experience, and yet if these were public buildings I am sure they would be strongly criticised. I will not mention any one, but non. gentlemen who have been about the city will no doubt have remarked some of them. At all events, we have thought it best, under all the circumstances, to place the responsibility for this work in the hands of our own staff. I may say to my hon. friend that before we reach the items for public buildings chargeable to capital account, I hope to place the plans upon the table for the inspection of the House.
The minister might give us an idea of the style of architecture.
I have not seen the plans as finally adopted by the chief architect. He has promised to have them ready for me in the course of a few days, when I will bring them before the House.

The Minister of Public Works has promised to perform all that is required of him by this House. Heretofore the plans of the various public buildings in the city of Ottawa have always been laid on the table of the House for our inspection. We are all, as the hon. member states, proud of the public buildings here in Ottawa, and we have always exercised the right to see the plans and to know what the Minister of Public Works intends to do in reference to them. Sometimes it has happened that opinions expressed in the House have had the 'effect of altering the plans. There is no blame to be attached to the Minister of Public Works because he did not adopt the plans he advertised for; he had prepared amended plans, which, he says, he will lay on the table of the House. He intends, before a vote is taken, submitting them to the House for our inspection.

I wish to ask a question which concerns the Postmaster General, and which refers to a report which appears in this morning's issue of the Ottawa ' Citizen,' and also of the Montreal ' Gazette.' The Postmaster General, speaking last night at the annual banquet of the Montreal branch of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, is credited with the following statement regarding the fiscal policy of this country:-
Our commercial ascendency, thanks to the wise fiscal policy adopted by this country twenty-five years ago, is the admiration of the world to-day.
I rise to ask the Postmaster General if he did make that statement, and if he does Mr. PUGSLEY.
consider that this country has had but one fiscal policy during the last twenty-five years.

My attention has been drawn to the report published in the Montreal * Gazette,' and in the Ottawa * Citizen.' I notice there is a difference between the report published in the French papers and that published in the English papers. In the Montreal French papers of this morning I am quoted as having said that it was the policy adopted fifteen years ago; and that is in fact what I said. There is only a difference in figures, the English papers have a two instead of a one. Besides I may say that there was no fiscal policy adopted twenty-five years ago, the policy of protection was adopted thirty-two years ago, and the only other policy since adopted was the Fielding tariff of 1897. If my hon. friend will read the remarks made by the leader of the opposition on the same occasion, he will find that the leader of the opposition spoke of my reference to the fiscal policy of fifteen years ago, and he said I should have gone a little further back to get at the origin of our fiscal policy- these are about his words-they have practised what we have been preaching.
When my hon. friend said fifteen years ago he was nearer right than he thought he was.
I do not wish to express any opinion, but merely to correct the statement.

A few moments ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) placed before you a motion to withdraw from the Order Paper two Bills, one relating to the manufacture of matches and the other relating to the importation of opium. We are not very sure whether these are the Bills he introduced last evening or whether they are the Bills that were introduced prior to his placing on the Order Paper the resolution on which they were based.
The Bills I asked to have withdrawn were those placed on the Order Paper prior to giving notice of the resolutions which were passed last night.

I would like to call the attention once more of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the depredations, regular and constant, of American poachers upon the fisheries on the coast of the province of British Columbia, and more particularly on the west coast of Vancouver island. I brought this matter to his attention on the 16th of December last, and

called attention to an article which had just appeared in the Victoria Daily ' Colonist,' in which it was stated that officers and passengers of a passing vessel were surprised to see a string of light extending from Raphael Point to Estevan.
These lights belonged to a number of American fishing vessels engaged in poaching. The minister at that time betrayed such lamentable ignorance of the geography of the locus in quo that he got the fisheries of Hecate Straits confounded with those on the west coast of Vancouver island. It is in hope that the minister has since become better acquainted with the question during the recess, and has further lasted himself upon the topography of the country and of the condition of the fisheries out there, that I venture to bring this matter up again to-day. I may say that the game still goes on. I have extracts from our own press and from the press in the United States, showing that what is complained of is not an occasional raid by these fishermen, but is a systematic business carried on by a number of Americans who are robbing us of our fisheries contrary to law. I propose to read a few extracts which will substantiate this position. I quote now from the ' Colonist ' of the. 29th December:
The steamer 'Tees' which returned from Quatsino Sound and way ports of the west coast yesterday morning with 25 passengers and a small cargo, including gillbone and fertilizer from the whaling stations, bronght news that poaching by United States vessels is being continued off the west coast of Vancouver island, where the poachers use the harbours freely. One of the fishing vessels was tied up near the whaling station at Kyuquot when the steamer 'Tees' passed, and another was in Sidney Inlet.
The Seattle ' Times,' a newspaper published in the city of Seattle says:-
Part of the anxiety felt over the safety of the individual vessels of the Seattle halibut fleet this morning

Mark you, Mr. Speaker, ' the Seattle halibut fleet'; that is the Seattle halibut fleet that poaches on the west coast of Vancouver island.
-was relieved by news brought by Captain Sam Larsen of the steamship 'Standard No. 2' that the gasoline fishing schooners, 'Lief E.,' 'Woodbury,' 'La Paloma' and 'MalolV were safe and sound when he left the grounds near Sidney Inlet Monday.
For the information of my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in case he does not know, I will tell him that Sidney Inlet is on the west coast of Vancouver Island.
The report made by the captain of the Standard Oil steamship, 'Col. E. L. Drake,' that he had seen the wreck of a halibut fishing vessel near Cape Flattery some days ago
l as caused anxiety about all vessels now absent from port.
I would like his attention to be given for a moment to this too:
Preparations now are being made for a number of gasoline schooners to leave within the next few days. Among those about to start are the 'Corona,' 'Roosevelt,' 'Northland,' 'Daisy' and 'Ida May.' The 'Ida May' possibly will be detained in getting away, as she has to have a new engine installed.
That is from a Seattle newspaper and is dated the 29th December. Again, on the 7th January, the following appears in the same paper, the Seattle ' Times '. I quote from the 'Colonist' of January 7, 1911:-
The Seattle 'Times' of yesterday tells of the departure of another fleet for Sidney Inlet.' The 'Times' says: The schooner 'Wiedling Bros.' arrived in port last night with 45,000 pounds of halibut, one of the largest catches recently reported. Together with the 'Northland,'-
The ' Northland ' is one of the boats mentioned in the ' Times ' of the 29th December.
-*' Annie Larsen ' and ' Sophie Jones,' the 'Wiedling Bros.' is preparing to sail again for the fishing banks. It is expected that the four vessels will get away from port sometime to-night. An attempt will he made first to fish off Cape Flattery, hut if the weather will not permit the vessels will proceed to Sidney Inlet.
I submit that these reports show that there are two fleets maintained in Seattle for the purpose of exploiting these fisheries, and the complaint I make is not of an occasional raid which my friends of the fishery protection service might possibly find it difficult to deal with,_ but of the systematic and organized, business in which there is a number of schooners employed all the year around. It is an outrage upon the people of British Columbia to think that this government is absolutely^ unable to cope with the situation. Some little explanation may be given of this. We have the explanation of Captain Newcombe of the ' Kestrel.' I may say, as I have before stated in this House, that the ' Kestrel ' is an ordinary fishery cruiser that Captain Newcombe has time and time and time again told the department of Marine and Fisheries is absolutely unfit for the service. She is too slow, she is not properly equipped and is absolutely useless for the service in which she is engaged. Captain Newcombe explains the reason why..he did not go to the west coast of Vancouver island. According to his own statement, if he had gone there, he would not have got any of these pirates, but probably he would have driven them away, because his boat is too slow to catch them. He says, according to a report in the ' Colonist ' newspaper.

The 'Kestrel's' orders have been, to cruise in Hecate straits, and although the depredations of the poaching vessels on the west coast of Vancouver island was known to her officers they were unable to proceed there, because in the first place their orders were explicit to remain in the north despite the fact that the poachers had changed their sphere of operations, and in the second place, the 'Kestrel' is not considered a suitable vessel for winter weather off the west coast of Vancouver island.
It cannot exactly be news to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to hear that the poachers were not to be expected in Hecate straits, but notwithstanding that fact, he ordered his cruiser to stay there and catch the poachers in a place where no poachers would go. I say that because I find in the report of the fisheries protection service of this year at page 353 that it is stated:
During the present season halibut has been extremely scarce in Hecate straits, and consequently the competition between fishermen very keen.
The fact of the matter is, that the Hecate straits fishing grounds have been seriously depleted by the depredations of the American fishermen. In the report of the department for the year 1908, I think, the minister, or his officers, states that halibut to the extent of 1,500,000 lbs, the value of which I have forgotten, was illegally taken from the banks of Hecate straits by American fishermen. That thing has been going on for a long time with the result that to-day the size of the halibut in Hecate straits has decreased to such an extent that it is no longer a desirable fishing ground, and fishermen have transferred their operations to the new banks which have been discovered on the west coast of Vancouver island. This matter is not new. We have, this year, Mr. John J. Williams, Inspector of Fisheries, complaining that the ' Falcon ' which was going to be kept on the ground, was inadequate for the purpose. We have had this matter taken up iri this House at various times and we had a most admirable speech made by Mr. Sloan, then member for Comox-Atlin, in which he went fully into this matter. We also had a speech from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries himself, on the subject, which will be found in ' Hansard ' of 1906-7, page 1777. He states there:-
I have found that there is a great deal of poaching done, especially on the western coast of Vancouver and within the three mile limit. If, how-ever, we have not the right to go outside the three mile limit in Hecate strait and Dixon entrance, I think we should adopt the policy of protecting our Canadian fisheries. We are very glad to see the American fishermen taking so much interest in our fisheries, but at the same time it is the duty of the government to protect those fisheries Mr. BARNARD.
and keep them for our Canadian citizens. As they belong to us, they should be exploited by us; and if American fishermen go there they should at least-as has been done in the case of a New Washington company- give us as much benefit as possible. But we must do on the Pacific coast what I have said should be done with regard to the Atlantic coast. I am free to admit, however, that there seems to be more business activity shown by Canadians on the British Columbia coast. _ Our financial institutions have been ii vesting large sums there, which is a condition of affairs I am glad to see. For my part, I am ready to take all the necessary steps to protect our fisheries along that coast. I have asked my colleagues to put at the disposal of my department another boat, a cruiser, which should be devoted almost exclusively to the protection of our fisheries. A sum is in the estimates for that purpose on which the House will be asked to vote; but I am sure, from the tenor of this discussion, that all the hon. members will be glad to co-operate with the government in that respect and give us the means of protecting our fisheries in the west, as we are doing in the east.
That was in 1906. In 1907, just before the general elections, the same vote was put in the estimates, but there is no cruiser yet. In 1909, shortly after the general election, I was informed by the minister that plans had been prepared for a cruiser, and I think he said that tenders had been called for. We have not got that cruiser yet, and apparently we are no nearer to having her than we were before. The hon. gentleman may say that the ' Rainbow ' is adapted for this purpose, and I understand that there was some kind of an arrangement that in addition to being used as a training ship the ' Rainbow ' was to be engaged in this service. However, the facts appear to be that these fishing boats lie so close inshore that the ' Rainbow,' with her heavy draught, would be useless for the service. The most suitable craft is a speedy gasoline boat of 20 or 25 knots, because these American fishing boats are all equipped with high power gasoline engines, and they can get out of the way of a steamer whose smoke they can see a great distance off. The fisheries of British Columbia to-day lead in productiveness the fisheries of the rest of the Dominion, and it is only in British Columbia that the revenues received bv the Dominion from the fisheries far exceeds the expenditure. Prof. Prince, in his report, states that the British Columbia fisheries are probably the finest in the world, and it is the undoubted right of the people of that province to demand from this government that these fisheries shall be protected from depletion by the depredations which are now going on. I ask that the government shall provide, in the estimates this year, an appropriation for one or two gasoline boats to he used in this protective service.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Some time ago my hon. friend (Mr. Barnard) read an article from a paper published in Victoria, and stated that there were depredations on the fisheries of British Columbia, and particularly on the west coast of Vancouver inland. The hon. gentleman has been trying to poke fun at me, because, as he hints, I am not familiar with the geography of the country, but I would point out to the hon. gentleman that he read the newspaper article in such a low voice that I could not hear it, and then, after reading the article, he referred especially to Hecate straits, which lead me to think that his remarks were directed particularly to these waters.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman was not listening.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: On the contrary, I was paying every attention, but unfortunately, I could not hear the hon. gentleman's reading, and sq, while part of my answers was directed to what I did hear, the other part may not have been appropriate to his question. If, when the hon. gentleman wishes to question me in future, he would give notice, I shall bring with me.all the papers in the matter and be better equipped to answer him than I can possibly be speaking on the spur of the moment. However, the hon. gentleman will find, from the public documents, that we have largely increased, in recent years, the fishery protective service on the British Columbia coast. Perhaps it is not yet as efficient as it should be in view of the very active development of the fisheries there and the necessity for properly protecting them. I think, however, that the new addition made to the fleet will enable us to cope with the situation more effectively. It is true, as stated by the hon. gentleman, that some years ago we had a vote in the estimates for the purchase of a vessel, but although we did not purchase a vessel then we did charter one for the special purpose of looking after the fisheries.
Was that the ' Wm. Jolliffc?'

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not remember the name of the vessel.
Is she not released from charter now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: If it was the ' Jolliffe ' I do not think she is now chartered.
Was there any other vessel chartered for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I do not keep all these details in my memory, and I cannot now recall. I may say that after the vote appeared in the estimates the plans had to be prepared, and we afterwards thought that we could purchase the ' Rainbow ' Notwithstanding what my hon. friend says, I think the ' Rainbow ' is suitable for doing a large part of this work. She may not be
able to enter certain waters where poachers are likely to be found, I do not think it advisable that poachers should be informed as to what our plans are, but I can assure my hon. friend that we are taking all the necessary steps to protect adequately the fisheries of the British Columbia coast.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether there is a close season when herring traps cannot be used, or does the season extend over the whole year? I desire also to ask him, what is the maximum length of the leader from the shore to the bowl of the trap? As I understand, the herring trap is one which takes all kinds of fish frequenting our waters, including mackerel and salmon, which are fish of great commercial value to Canada. With respect to salmon, there is a close season, when Canadians fishing in purely Canadian waters cannot take them even under license, and I would like to ask the minister, can the American or Canadian, as the case may be, fish for salmon on the Labrador coast, or the Magdalen Islands coast at a season when it. is not legal to take salmon in the other coastal waters of the Gulf of St. Lawrence? This is a very important matter which may very seriously affect the fishing interests in purely Canadian waters. I quite realize that the concessions given to our United States friends are equal to those given to Canadians who go to fish in those dual waters; but at the same time I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that licensing the American citizen gives him a prior right in placing his trap, and, as I understand, the leader of this trap extends practically to the shore, so that to all intents and purposes he has privileges which a Canadian has not in purely Canadian waters. For example, I understand that mackerel traps are practically prohibited along the St. Lawrence coast. There is one on the north coast of Prince Edward Island, but it is the only one, so far as I am aware, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. It is under a heavy license fee, and it was there for many years before the licensing plan was in vogue. So that mackerel traps are practically not allowed in the purely Canadian coastal waters of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, whereas we are now licensing, in the coast waters of Labrador and the Magdalen Islands, a trap which is to all intents and purposes a mackerel trap, and which will also take salmon, which I believe frequent those waters, especially the Labrador coast, in large quantities, and at a season when our own fishermen are not allowed to take them. I think it only fair that the minister's attention should be brought to these facts.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I do not know whether my hon. friend has seen the regulations

which have been adopted as a result of the negotiations with the United States authorities; but I can assure him that all the fears he expresses as to rights being given to Americans which are not going to be enjoyed by Canadians, may be discarded. There has been no change in the regulations which will in any shape or form be prejudicial to the salmon industry or to Canadian fishermen. The regulations which provide for a close season for salmon are still maintained, and the regulations which provide that traps must be made in such a way as not to affect the ascent of the salmon are also maintained. The changes, which are not of great importance, my>
hon. friend calls concessions to the Americans. The right we have given to Americans to get licenses is not a concession granted by us. It is a right which they had under the treaty of 1818. As a matter of fact, they were claiming that they had an absolute right to fish in those waters without any license at all. The hon. Minister of Justice quoted yesterday a despatch sent by the Foreign Office in 1906 to the effect that Newfoundland, and it applied also to Canada, had no right under that treaty to impose any license fee on American fishermen. That treaty gives them the right to fish on the Labrador coast and the Magdalen Islands coast in common with British subjects, and it was contended by the American authorities that we could not impose upon them a restriction in the form of a license. This claim certainly deserves a great deal of consideration, and, as the Minister of Justice said yesterday, was accepted by the Foreign Office. 'So I thought the other day, when the American authorities were willing to accept a license from us, thus virtually recognizing our right to issue a license, it was something of the utmost importance to Canada, because our licensing system is of great value for the preservation of our fisheries. The American experts who were there, after hearing the reasons adduced in favour of maintaining our licensing system, considered it a very fair one which is tantamount to their admission that the way we have been managing our fisheries is certainly commendable. My hon. friend asks what length will be the leaders. It was provided in the regulations, previous to the agreement made the other day, that all the leaders should start from the shore. The American authorities contended with a great deal of reason-I think they were right in that respect-that this was prejudicial to their rights on the treaty coast, because if our regulations provided that all the leaders should start from the shore, and if they had no right to go to the shore under the treaty, they meant that they could not put traps there where Canadians were permitted to put them, which would be discriminating. This struck me as a Mr. BRODEUR.
fair contention, and we tried to meet it by declaring that if the leader should start from the shore, then the length would be determined by our * fishery officers and not by anybody else, and our officers determine the length of the leader by the depth of the water. I think that by all these changes which have been made my hon. friend may feel assured that we have not departed in any shape or form from the principle underlying our regulations, and that the mackerel as well as the salmon fisheries will be just as well preserved under the changes made as they were under the regulations which existed before.

The minister has said that the length of the leader is to be determined by the fishery officer. Should the applicant say I want a leader only 100 yards from the shore, then the trap must be at the end of the leader, which would be simply one hundred yards from the shore. That is a point worthy of consideration. Regarding the protection of our salmon, the minister tells us that the close season will not be changed. That is not the question with me, as I understand it. The season for fishing the herring traps is all the year round, if the owner could fish all the year in spite of the weather. Therefore, if a trap catches salmon, and the owner is allowed to use the salmon, there is practically no close season for the salmon caught in the trap.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Any fish caught in the close season contrary to the regulations is supposed to be caught illegally, and has to be thrown away.

I understood the minister to say that certain regulations had been framed as the result of this memo entered into by the American and Canadian authorities. If that is the case, may I ask whether those will be available to members and when w'e can have them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: They will be brought dtfwn Monday.
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.

The hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) asked that the item relating to the Montreal barracks should stand, so we will pass to the Ontario items.
Public Works-Buildings, Ontario-Athens public building, $5,000.

I find that the postal revenue of this town last year was $2,152.63, money orders issued, $17,482.56, money orders paid $9,630.94. The population two years ago was 1,000. It is quite a rapidly growing town, has six churches, fourteen stores, two hotels, lumber mill and two planing mills and woollen factory among other industries. This will not complete.
Is this just for a post office?
Yes. Mv instructions to the chief architect are to keep the cost of this building in the vicinity of $13,000 or $14,000. It will not exceed $15,000.
Does that include the site?

Yes.
Mr. 'CROSBY. Has the hon. minister had any requisition from the Post Office Department for this building as being required for the work of the department?

Not from the Post Office Department. I may say, however, that my attention was called by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), in whose constituency this town is situated, to the very great need of post office accommodation there. My hon. friend no doubt is aware that the department allows a small amount to the postmaster to enable him to secure accommodation. The people of Athens have been urging, so the Minister of Railways informs me, that increased accommodation be given them, and he hoped it would be possible to make an arrangement with a banking company which was going to erect a building there so that my department should pay a portion of the rent necessary to get increased accommodation. However, the matter fell through, and I decided to ask for a vote for a building not to cost a great deal of money but one that would be suitable to the needs of the town.
Here is a post office erected solely for the business of the Post Office Department. After it is erected who pays for the renting expenses of that building ?
The Department of Public Works.
Is that the case all through ?
Yes.

The Department of Public Works does not require a building, but the minister, without consultation with the Postmaster General erects a post office building for post office business and then assumes the cost of that building after its erection. Does the rental now paid for post office accommodation there fall into the revenue of the post office?

No, that rental will cease. I have sometimes thought it might not be undesirable, certainly it would not be from the standpoint of my department, if the other departments would pay the Public Works Department a rental for buildings which we erect forythem.

Under the present system when the Postmaster General goes before the country and presents his accounts, saying this is my revenue, and this my expenditure, he is not making a fair exhibit to the country.
I would not like to say that.

He is shouldering a portion of the expense of his department on another department, and concealing it, in effect, in that other department. I have no hesitation in saying that, in my mind, the Minister of Public Works ought not to undertake to erect a building for another department until requisitioned by that department. This slipshod method is carried on simply for patronage purposes. Two ministers who have nothing to do with the post office decide to build a building for the Postmaster General and the carrying out of his business.
Rather for the public accommodation.
I think that is bad policy
No, in this case, it is for the public accommodation.

If the Minister of Railways should some morning find the Minister of Public Works building a station somewhere on the Intercolonial railway, and on its completion this should relieve the Minister of Railways of the cost of maintaining that station, and then when the Minister of Railways presented his balance sheet to the country, he omitted the cost of that station, he would be giving a wrong account of part of the expenses of his department. I think the minister of post offices, the Postmaster General, ought to pursue exactly the same course as the Minister of Railways in this matter, and that he should not have the Minister of Public Works bearing the cost of part of the accommodation required by his department.

My hon. friend makes two points, one that we should not erect a building for another department without a requisition from the minister of that department, and the other, that if we do erect a post office the Postmaster General should pay a rental for it. Since when did my hon. friend entertain these views.
For a good many years.
Certainly not before 1896.
For the last 7 or 8 years I have advocated them steadily in the House.

I used to have a good deal of respect for the views of my hon. friend and have now, but I cannot find

that when my hon. friend was Minister of Finance, and had a powerful influence in the disposition of public moneys, he ever advocated any such idea as he is now putting forward. There is much to be said in favour of the views he has advanced and . if he were coming here for the first time to get us to lay down a course to be pursued, irrespective of what has been done in the past, I think he would find me favourable to his views, but the difficulty is, that if- we are to compel the ministers of the different departments to pay rentals for the buildings occupied by them, it would greatly disturb the accounts of the departments and for purposes of comparison with previous years, the accounts would become valueless. I would be very glad if something of the kind could be done, because it would show my department as a good revenue producer. For instance, if I could get a rental of even 3 per cent on the Montreal post office, which cost $1,000,000, it would be $30,000 a year which would be quite a revenue of itself fqy my department, and if that were multiplied by the revenues of post offices, &c., all over the country, it would make a very good showing. The difficulty is, that that has been contrary to the principle which has been pursued, not only ever since confederation, but ever since the provinces of Canada were inhabited, ever since we had public buildings. The erection and maintenance of public buildings has always been cast upon the Department of Public Works, and it is very difficult to make these changes. I have suggested to my hon. friend the Postmaster General that it would not be a bad idea if he would take into consideration, and pay for the use of the post offices throughout the country, a fair rental, based upon the interest on cost. So far, he has not been able to agree with the suggestion I have made, only made in a tentative manner. If the member for North Toronto could nersuade the Postmaster General and the Minister of Customs to adopt his view, certainly 1 would not object. But after all, it would not make much difference to the country, because it would be simply taking the cost out of one branch and paying it on behalf of other branches.

If the Postmaster General is anxious to give to the people of this country the very best postal service he can. and in the most economical way, he will study the question a good deal' before he *would requisition the Minister of Public Works to build a large number of these post offices, which the Minister of Public Works is now building for merely patronage reasons. Consequently, this country would be saved a very large amount of 'money, which the Postmaster General might well use to extend and improve the postal ser-Mr. PUGSLEY.
vice. If a building is to be erected for the purpose of a post office the Postmaster General and the postal authorities ought to be the judges whether it is necessary or not. What does the Postmaster General want to give to. the people of Athens? He wants to give them facilities for getting their mails in and out, he is doing it and can still do it, as they do on principle in the United States, in ninety-nine out of one hundred cases. He can give it to them by way of rental rather than by -way of spending a large amount of money in expensive public buildings, and the people will get as good service, and the department will have the revenue to enlarge and cheapen the service of the country generally.

These public buildings are also used for other purposes. Generally, when the construction of a public building is decided upon by the Minister of Public Works, we select our space, we give our opinion of the space we will require in that building and that locality. The Minister of Inland Revenue is consulted likewise. I may mention, for illustration, the case of Nicolet, where I myself advocated the construction of the post office. Whilst the revenue of the town of Nicolet would not justify the construction of a building for a post office alone, yet we had to consider that there was a regiment stationed there, and they wanted a certain amount of space for armoury purposes. Then there was the customs and excise office to be provided for. Therefore, my hon. friend must not apply his remarks to the post office alone; he must consider all the other departments that use the building.

If you have in view economy alone, you could house half a dozen departments in the same building. The fact in this case is that the Postmaster General has never requisitioned for the purpose of his department to have a public building put up at Athens.

The name of the place is familiar to me as being a historical name, and I remember well that the request has often been made by the people of the locality for a post office. I do not want to bring politics into this matter, but I think Athens is in a county represented by an hon. gentleman of the opposition. I mention this to show that politics have nothing to do with the erection of this building.

What I am trying to bring out is the method on which these buildings are erected. Here is a minister who has nothing to do with the Post Office Department, and who is putting up a building without the request of the Postmaster General, with no hint from the Post Office Department that the work is necessary for that department. Now, I say that is not a proper principle. Take another and a more

signal instance, the instance of Hampton, N.B., in the county of Kings, that I formerly represented I was surprised, the other morning, in reading the ' Hansard,' to find a vote had been given for a public building in Hampton, and that the minister had declared that ^Hampton had a population of 2,000, that it was a remarkably live place, and a growing place, and so he persuaded the House to give him a vote of $5,000 as a starter for a post office.

It appears that the Postmaster General is not interested in what post office buildings are erected. He is not consulted when a post office is to be erected although it would only seem natural that he would be the very first person that would be consulted.
I am.

You were not consulted
in this case?
No, $3,000 as a starter, the whole thing to cost not more than $5,000.

Now, I was anxious to know whether the Postmaster General had represented to the Minister of Public WotEs that for the purpose of his work it was necessary to have a $5,000 building put up in Hampton.

This may have occurred during my absence. But I am sure the department must have been consulted.
Mr. FOSTER I would like the minister to find out and bring down the information. I would like to know whether the minister, who is, I think, disposed to be economical, requisitioned that building, or whether he thought it was necessary.
May 1 ask the Minister of Public Works if the Minister of Railways and Canals did not consult him in regard to this matter?
Yes.
And it is also in the constituency of the Minister of Railways and Canals?

Well, it is in the county of Leeds, but I think a part of Leeds forms a portion of the constituency of Brockville. My impression is that it is in the constituency of the Minister of Railways and Canals.
Is not the minister perfectly aware that there is a portion of Leeds in the constituency of Brockville?
No I am not, but that is my belief.
Of course, there is no politics in this.
Part of it is in Brockville.
That is what I understand.
This $5,000 is for a constituency represented by the Minister of Railways and Canals, and it is to be followed with another vote of $10,000 making about $15,000.
Not exceeding that.
Many sessions ago.

I understood the Minister of Public Works to say that this vote was asked for this particular building without consulting the Postmaster General, and without any requisition from the Postmaster General for the building. The Minister of Public Works explicitly stated the other night that it would not be expected that the Department of Public Works should consult the Postmaster General with regard to the erection of post offices in this country.
My hon. friend is wrong. As to the accommodation required for post offices I stated that we did consult the Post Office Department.
I said nothing with regard to the accommodation for post offices at all.

With regard to the architecture and the building of the office-no. Of course, that is a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works, but the first requisition always comes from the Post Office Department.

Well, that is perfectly contrary to the statement made by the Minister of Public Works the other night because he said that he was endeavouring to get the Postmaster General to consider these matters with him. Does the Post, master General think it is dealing fairly with the people of this country for $15,000 to be spent for the erection of a post office in Athens, or in any other village the size of Athens when there are whole townships in Ontario that have no post office within their bounds? Does he think it is fair today to spend $15,000 for a post office for a village the size of this when there are people in country places who have to travel all the way from five miles to twelve and fifteen miles to get their mail? He must agree that it is not fair play, and if he is not consulted in regard to the money being spent for the erection of post offices he should be and he should use his influence to see that the public get the postal facilities of which they stand in need. He should take a special interest in this because he is the man to whom they look for ' redress in these matters.

In answer to my hon. friend's question, I would say that there is no analogy whatever in my judgment between the case of a town and that of a whole township. In the town the population is concentrated at a given spot. There may be 2,000 or 3,000 or 5,000 people congregated together, but in a whole township the population is scattered. You could not erect one building for a whole township while you could for a town even though the population might be less than that of the whole township. As regards postal facilities in a whole township, I do not know that there is any reason why the people should not be provided with these postal facilities where the distance is about five miles from a post office. It is certainly the policy of the Post Office Department to grant any request which is made with such a distance in view. Whenever my hon. friend on behalf of his own township in Frontenac or any other non. gentleman makes a request to provide postal facilities, where there is a distance of about five miles, the Post Office Department cannot but accede to that request, and I appeal to him and to members of the House on both sides whether, whenever a request- of that kind is made to the Post Office Department, it is not granted.

I am very glad indeed that I intervened in this discussion, because I have got a very important statement in so far as my constituency is- concerned from the Postmaster General. I am very glad he has made that statement, and I can assure him that the time will be exceedingly short when I shall appear before him and ask him to carry out to the letter the statement which he has placed on ' Hansard ' this afternoon.
Did we not live up to it in the past?
No, the Post Office Department has not lived up to it.
Can my hon. friend cite an instance in his county, where, within a distance of five or six miles, there are no postal facilities?	*
Yes, I will cite an instance. Last year, or the year before
I know this case; be very careful.

Yes, I will be careful. Thus far I have made no statement which I have had to retract. I made a request for a post office between Sharbot Lake and Maberly. I have in my possession now the answer which I obtained from the Postmaster General in regard to that matter. There was a settlement of 20 or 22 families. The nearest any of them lived to a post office was from 5 to 8 miles.
Five to eight miles.

Yes, five to eight miles. They asked for a bi-weekly service. They were satisfied with a mail twice a week. I have the letter in my possession from the Postmaster General, in which he said that it would cost $70 to deliver the mail twice a week to this settlement, that it would cost $35 for the postmaster's salary, making a total of $105, that the revenue would not possibly exceed $10 or $15 a year, and that he did not feel that his department would be justified in expending the sum of $90 a year since there were only 20 or 22 families interested. That is a case in point to which I refer, and I am glad that the Postmaster General has put himself on record pn ' Hansard ' here to-day to the effect that his department is willing to grant postal facilities in country places where they have to go five miles or more for their mail.
Is it a case of infrequency of service or the need of an office?

They want an office; they have no service at all. They would be satisfied with a service twice a week which, I think, is a very mild request on their part. I do not want to simply criticise these items when they come up but I do think I would not be fair to my constituents if I allowed votes of large sums of money for post offices in cities and towns to go through here and put up no protest on behalf of the country districts where they have very meagre, and in some cases, no postal facilities whatever. I recognize that in large cities like Montreal and Toronto and some others, and in very large and enterprising towns it would be expected that there should be better facilities than in country districts, but I believe it .is entirely unwarranted that,, large sums of money should be spent in these smaller towns while the country districts, where the people have to go five and ten and twelve miles to get their mail, have to come here begging for a twice-a-week service.

I have several times expressed it in this House as my opinion that in a place where no reasonable accommodation for a post office can be obtained by renting it may become necessary for the government to provide that accommodation, by erecting a building, but where a building can be rented, as in this case, at a moderate cost of $125 a year, including fuel and light, to incur an annual expenditure of $1,300 is altogether wrong. I do not think such a policy can be justified before any intelligent people. The minister told us that Athens was a rapidly growing place and that the population is
2097.

1,000, but the fact is that while it is a good business centre the revenue there is only $2,151. Now, in looking down this list I find that there are many places which contribute a much larger revenue to the government and which have not a post office building and are not asking for one. Acton gives a revenue of $3,600 a year and it has no post office; Allison gives a revenue of $2,365 a year and we get a building there for $175 per annum, fuel and light included. Alvinston gives a revenue of over $2,000, Arthur a revenue of $2,600, Aurora a revenue of $4,000 fnearly twice as large as Athens), and Aylmer West a revenue of $6,800, and none of these places have post offices.
Aylmer is strongly urging for one.

In view of the fact that "there are so many of these towns that give a larger revenue than Athens and which have no post offices, there must be some reason for building a post office at Athens other than the needs of the public service. At one time Athens was in the constituency of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), and then we never heard anything about erecting a post office there, but it is taken into the constituency of the Minister of Railways and immediately a post office is to be erected. It would look as if the government had determined that only in favoured spots represented by their supporters will they erect these public buildings.
What department now pays the $125 a year rent for the present post office at Athens?
The Post Office Department.
And when this building is erected the Post Office Department will pay nothing?
No.

It is no wonder the Postmaster General would like to see post office buildings erected by the government, because he is relieved of paying rent, and his revenue is consequently increased. Since I have been in the House I have never h.eard of a post office building being erected anywhere except through the influence of some members supporting the government, and I suppose it is hardly any use to condemn that bad principle now. The Minister of Public Works must have been misled when he told us that Athens was in the riding of the hon. member for Leeds, because, as a matter of fact, it is in the constituency represented by the Minister of Railways. I have no doubt it is the same in this case as in many others. The Minister of Railways wants to have a post office in 67
that particular district, and some other day the Minister of Public Works may want to get something in his department, and so he gives a post office. In that way there is reciprocity between the ministers, and sometinj^s with members. As far as I am personally concerned, I would be glad to see a post office built in every village in the Dominion of Canada if we could afford it, but there is no policy laid down by the government in this matter, as we find post offices built in places much smaller in population and in revenue than other places which have no post office building. It is gratifying to find the Postmaster General stating that no request will be refused by him, so that we are in hopes of getting all the post offices we require.

I would like to give the Postmaster General an opportunity to make clear one or two points with reference to the new post office built at Athens. Did the Post Office Inspector for that district report complaining of the inadequacy of the accommodation already provided at that village, or suggesting that better accommodation should be provided? If he did make such a report, was any attempt made to rent a more commodious place?

I have not the papers to enable me to give my hon. friend the answer to-day. I may give it to him at the next sitting of the House.

amount as a contribution to the city of Brantford for a pavement and storm sewers, one-half of each.

I would say, for the information of the hon. minister, that the Brantford drill hall is not a building of ancient date. The first building, a wooden structure, dates back to 1868, but in 1895 some $10,000 was contributed ito enable local parties to erect a new drill hall, and in 1904 a contract was let for the construction of this building, amounting to $25,750, with further contracts for heating and electric wiring of $2,600 and $2,450 respectively. The total expenditure on the building from 1903-4 to 1910 was $49,311.43, to which add the $900 asked for in this item, and you have a cost of $50,200, or pretty nearly double the contract price. A few days ago my hon. friend spoke of the final cost of these drill halls and armouries compared with the contract price. On that occasion I said, on page 1628 of 'Hansard':-
If you take up the whole list of armouries from one end of the country to the other you will see that the actual cost, when the buildings are completed, runs from 25 to 75 per cent higher than the contract price, so that the estimated cost does not cut any figure at all.	.
For the information of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, I am prepared to substantiate the statement I made on that occasion, and to prove that the cost of the drill halls and armouries constructed in this country since 1896-the final cost.- has been from twenty-five to seventy-five per cent higher than the contract price, not only in one or two but in dozens of cases, and not. in one province alone, but in every province. Let me give him one or two instances, I might refer to the drill hall at Baddeck, N.S. Contract price was $3,750, and the cost $5,795.
For what portion of the work?
If the hon. minister wants to take it in that way, it makes it all the worse for himself.
That is the only way in which you can take it.
When I take the contract price, I mean the price of the contractor for the main part of the work, and the additional contracts for heating, lighting, &c. Is that satisfactory?
Yes.
With regard to Baddeck I find that the final cost, was some 59 per cent higher than the contract price.

Of course I have not here the details of the building at Baddeck, and it is very inconvenient to have to go Mr. PUGST EY-
into matters with regard to which I cannot be supposed to have the information with me. My hon. friend says the contract includes the building, heating, plumbing, fittings and everything of that kind. How is the additional amount made up?
The hon. minister is. certainly putting a conundrum to me.
I thought so.

He asked me to tell how the additional price is made up. We have had a good many instances-I have one in my mind now, the construction of a building near Kingston-in which I venture to say it w'ould puzzle the hon. genue-man himself to find out how the additional cost was made up.
What was the total amount paid for Baddeck drill hall?

According to a return dated the 8th April, 1910, and which was ordered on the 15th December, 1909, the total cost was $5,975.62. I presume that return gave the cost down to the 8th April, 1910. What has been expended since I cannot say.

Chesley public building, $15,000.

This is to make provision for the erection of a public building in the town of Chesley. I may say that the land has been purchased. It consists of a lot 104 by 104 on the west side of Main street, in the town of Chesley. The estimated cost of the building is not to exceed $15,000, that is, apart from the site, but including heating, plumbing and fittings. In 1901 the town had a population of 1,734. The information I have is that the town consists of 8 churches, 2 bank agencies, a woollen mill, sash and door factory, grist mill, saw mill, furniture factory, 3 hotels, 28 stores and a printing office. The revenue last year was $5,106, being a good increase on the year before. The building is required for a post office and custom house, also to afford accommodation as an armoury for the local militia company.
Have plans been prepared?
Plans have been prepared, and are now with the Post Office Department for consideration, and, we trust, approval.

Permit me to suggest that the contract should be let at as early a date as possible, so that the work may be proceeded with during the coming summer. In the year 1908, $5,000 was put in the estimates for the erection of this building, so the minister cannot be accused of any undue haste in the matter. Speaking on this subject in 1909, the minister assured me that the work of erecting the building would be proceeded with as soon as possible. In view of the large increase in the public revenue during the past year I expect that the minister will proceed with the work of erecting the building at an early date.

I am very glad that my hon. friend differs from many hon. gentle-Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
men opposite in thinking that it is entirely right and proper to erect a public building in a town of 1,700 population. I quite agree with him and that is why I put the item in. I believe it will be in the public interest, the town is a good one, and I am entirely prepared to completely justify the erection of a public building there.

The town of Chesley has increased in population very rapidly. That was ten years ago and the population may be a thousand more now.

I am very glad to know that. At the close of the last session of parliament, there was a large number of buildings provided for and much more than the chief architect, with his staff could undertake within quite a number of months. He has to take them up, one after another ; they cannot all be done at once. In the case of Chesley, tire plans are now in the department of the Postmaster General for approval. This contract for Dresden was just let a few days ago.

If the minister would recall the principle he laid down in the first session of 1909, there would be no difficulty in answering the question whether he had the record or not. The -minister laid it down then, that public buildings that were appropriated for, in the previous year's estimates, that is, in the pre-election year's estimates, would be gone on with before any other buildings were commenced. So that, if the minister remembered the principle he laid down and desired to follow it and knew that he had followed it, he would be certain that this building must have been appropriated fox-in the pre-election year. Otherwise it would be a violation of his pledge to go ahead with it before the building immediately preceding which certainly was first appropriated for in 1908. Consequently, the minister must, besides foregetting the first year when it was appropriated for, also have forgotten the pledge which he made in 1909.

My hon. friend does not state what I said correctly. What I said was that, before asking parliament for appropriations for new buildings, speaking as a general thing, we would ask parliament to appropriate moneys for buildings which had been contained in the estimates of 1907-8.
Is the minister quite sure that is what he said ?
Yes, I think so.
I have not 'Hansard' here.
At all events, that is what I ought to have said.
We will test our respective memories as soon as I can get * Hansard.'

I think that must be what I said. If I did not say that, it would

be a slip of the tongue. Immediately par-[DOT] liament votes money, all buildings stand on an equal footing.

I have noticed this custom which has been prevalent of late years and it is a very pernicious one. Items are "voted year after year for public works and nothing is done. I do not know whether it is as bad this year as last, or the year before. That, in my judgment, is a, very bad principle. The buildings are really required or they are not. If they are required, and the money is voted, the contract ought to be gone on with, and the expenditure made within the estimate. It is no justifiable excuse in the world to say that your architects are busy. If you had only a sufficient number of architects to prepare the plans for a quarter of the number of buildings, and we voted money for the other three quarters, would it be any justification for the government's conduct, in leaving over three quarters of the buildings for ten years and not starting them at all ? That is practically what the Minister of Public Works says now. If they are not going on with these buildings, why should the government get the .money for them ? In my opinion, we should only vote sufficient money each year to prepare the plans and to provide for the work that is proceeded with in that year. Then, we would not have, as we frequently have, these items standing over until an election comes on when they are held out as a bribe to electors to return a supporter of the government. The present system is pernicious and should not be tolerated by the House.
The contract in Dresden has been let and I said that the plans were actually all prepared for Chesley-post office and were in the hands of the Post Office Department for approval.
Why is the contract let for Dresden and not for Chesley? Is it not because the one is represented by a supporter of the government and the other is not?
My hon. friend is wrong, not as he usually is but as he sometimes is. Either one of us is stupid and probably I am
You ought to know best.

My hon. friend is so much older than I that I hope he won't be severe on me. We go on with the plans as the staff is able to get them ready, and as the department interested in the building approves we call for tenders.

Why is it that the plans are ready for one' place and the contract Mr. PUGSLEY.
let, and why are the plans not ready for the other place although the money was voted in the same year?

The case is stronger than my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) puts it because the vote for Chesley was taken in 1908, a year before the vote for Dresden was taken, and yet the site for the Chesley post office has not been purchased yet.
Yes it is.

Then if the site has been purchased it must have been paid for previous to last year because there is $15,000 asked, which is altogether a revote. But if the minister is right, the site for Chesley post office was purchased two years ago and nothing has been done since. One place is given the advantage of at least a year over the other.

The plans cannot be prepared until the site has been procured, and it happens in this case that the site for Dresden was ordered to be purchased on the 17th of August, 1908-so that there has been delay in the constituency, represented by Mr. Gordon, who supports the government-whereas the site for Chesley was not acquired until February, 1909.
All the evidence tends to show that this appropriation has been dangled before the people of that constituency for at least four years.

The minister tells us that his architects are not able to get out the plans for all these buildings in good time, and perhaps I can suggest to him a remedy for the delay. A grea(t many of these buildings are erected in towns ranging from 1,500 to 2,500 population; practically about the same sizedl buildings are called for; there is a great! deal of uniformity about them, and would it not be well for the minister to have standard plans and specifications which might be used for say twenty different towns, and thus save time and trouble and expense, and expedite the erection of the buildings.

That idea has often been thought of in the department, but the difficulty is that the style of architecture that is suited to the general surroundings of one town will not be suitable in another, and we find that it would not please the people to have one standard building for all sections of the country. Then, some towns are growing rapidly, especially in the west. The style of building must also have some reference to the location of the site. All these things have to be taken into consideration.
Dundas public building, $15,000.

We have purchased the lot, which has a frontage of 125 feet by a depth of one hundred and six feet, and we are at work on the plans. The building is to be used for post office, customs and inland revenue purposes, and the total cost will run up to probably $30,000. Dundas is quite an important town. It has a population of about 3,000 and several factories, and growing rapidly.
This is another instance in which the money was voted last year, and yet there was apparently no need of voting it. It would relieve the House of some work if we cut out all these votes.
We had a great deal of difficulty in getting the site. It was only recently that we got it. The wife of the owner refused until recently to sign away her dower.
When was the first vote taken for this building?

In 1907-8.
Elora publio building, $14,000.

This is under contract. The building is to cost $12,949. We paid $380 for the site. The fittings, furniture, lock boxes, sidewalk, fencing and contingencies will bring the total estimated cost up to $19,413.61. The site has a frontage of 69 feet by a depth of 132 feet. The population in_1901 was about 1,200, and I believe it is growing.
That vote was first taken in 1907-8 also, I believe?
Yes.

I find that the votes for all these smaller places-Preston, Dundas, Elora, Essex, Fergus, Harriston/ Mitchell, Midland, Mount Forest, Seaforth, Goderich, Wallaceburg, Wiarton-were all taken in 1907-8, just before the general election, and nothing practically has been done since.

My hon. friend surely does not forget that in 1908-9 there was a great decline in the revenue, and we made an appeal to parliament to justify us in allowing all except the most urgent public works to stand over, which parliament readily agreed to do. I remember that our friends were called together, and they all said they would not press for even urgent public buildings until the revenues got into better condition.
If the hon. gentleman looks back to the year 1903-4, just before another general election, and the year following, he will find just the same state of things existing.

I was not here in 1903-4.
Essex post office, $14,000.

The site has been acquired at a cost of $1,000. The contract has not been let, but the plans are now before the Post Office Department for approval. We expect the total cost to be $15,-
000.
Is Elora a shire town?

No, it is not, but the people there were complaining very bitterly of the want of accommodation, and in view of the fact that it has an excellent waterpower, that its manufacturing is developing -carriage, sash and door factories, agricultural implement factories, saw and grist mills-that it has a large number of stores, and that it is the centre of a very beautiful country, we thought we might make an exception and give it a public building that would be suitable to a town of that size and with such a fine future.
I understand that one of the qualifications for getting a post office is having water-power.
That is incidental to growth and development.
Another is to have a certain number of stores.
Yes.
And another is to have one or two railways, and still another that the people should urge it very strongly.
Yes, think of the revenue, $3,500 last year.

That is not a big revenue. I have pointed out other towns with larger revenue which have not been thus favoured. I have in mind other towns which have all these qualifications, and requisites and more.
The town of Milton, for instance.
I am not complaining, but if I can bring that town of mine within the scope of all these various qualifications-
The friends of my hon. friend would all fight very hard against it.

In that case I would fight them. I notice that the minister does not forget the town of Milton. He brings it up every time I rise so that evidently his conscience is rather uncomfortable, and I want to keep him in that frame of mind until he does justice to the town of Milton.

If my hon. friend from Halton" (Mr. Henderson) thinks that the

sensitive conscience of the Minister of Public Works is likely to compel him to do justice, I am afraid he will be sadly disappointed. I would never have credited the hon. minister with possessing any such conscience. What amused me was the answer which he gave with regard to the building in Elora, namely, that the people pressed for it very hard. Yet the vote was put nearly four years ago, and the plans are not ready yet.

My hon. friend must not jump to conclusions so quickly. He said the plans are not even under way. Why, the construction is well under way to-day. Let me say why 1 am pleased with my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). From the way in which he has developed along the line of the necessity for public buildings, I look forward to the day when he will have persuaded all our friends opposite into his own conviction, and we will find them approving every item in the estimates for public buildings.
Fergus public building, $14,000.
What county?
Wellington South.
How far from Elora?
Let me first give the population. It was 1,396 nine years ago. Fergus also has an excellent water-power. It has an .iron foundry, a planing mill, two saw mills, a factory for split peas, &c.
How many churches?
Seven.
I thought so. It is a Scotch town.
And the people have been urging very strongly to have this building built.
What is the postal revenue?
$4,300, money orders issued $12,633, money orders paid $20,614.
What is the estimated cost?

The contract is for $13,449, cost of site $700, fittings, furniture, lock boxes, sidewalks, fencing, &c., will bring the total to $19,556, comprising everything.
Fort William public building, enlarging,
That is for the purpose of making additions to the post office owing to the rapidly increasing business.

What will the additions cost?
Mr. SPROULE

$7,450 is contract price.
Gananoque post office, addition, $4,000.

That is to build an addition to the main building, the addition will be 22 feet by 24-a one story brick building. We have got the land for the purpose from the town as a gift. The 'surveying and legal expenses cost us $75, the erection of the building $2,500, the alterations and fittings $1,500 making a total of $4,075. The specifications are now in the hands of the printer, and we will call for tenders as soon as they are ready.

A moment ago the minister challenged the accuracy of my recollection as to the statement made by him in the session of 1909, and which, if he meant it, would have constituted a principle for his department to follow in the construction of these public 'buildings. I said that the Minister of Public Works had clearly stated that such public buildings as were in the 1908 estimates and which he was not able to go on with in 1909, by reason of what he called his retrenchment policy, would be gone on with before any others were initiated. The hon. minister contradicted that statement. I have the ' Hansard ' here which will show which of us was correct. At page 1300 of the ' Hansard ' of 1909, I asked him the following question :
Will the minister also give us the assurance that those public buildings which were in the estimates last year and which now are unfortunately discontinued will be preferred and gone on with before other public buildings of a similar kind are initiated?
The minister replied :
I think that is a very fair question. I feel that is the course that I should pursue as Minister of Public Works, and will certainly recommend to my colleagues.
That- was perhaps as pronounced a statement as the minister was ever tempted to make in Committee of Supply. He went on to say :
Of course, there may be cases arise, such as a public building being burned down or a wharf being carried away, which might create an exception, and we might have to include these new works, but as a general principle I am and would be committed to those works which parliament was asked to sanction last year.
The only exception the minister could think of was a public building burned down or a wharf carried away; that would be, I presume, a wharf built where there is water. A few moments ago a public building in Chesley was referred to. That public building was not in the estimates for 1908. Then a public building in Dresden was spoken of, which was in the estimates for 1908, and each year since. Under tha min-

ister's ruling, under his solemn pledge to the House and the country, because that quotation was largely circulated through the press, the minister would be bound to go on with the public building in Chesley before he even initiated a public building in Dresden. Now, in 1910, the minister is further ahead with the public building in Dresden than with that in Chesley, indeed, his department has been inactive and has done nothing in regard to the Chesley building. It would be interesting for this committee to have the minister exercise his well known and most admirable ingenuity in explaining the consistency of his course with that principle.

Let me correct an error into which my hon. friend inadvertently fell. He said the Chesley building was not in the estimates of 1908. He should have said the opposite. Chesley was in the estimates of 1907-8, while Dresden was not.
Mr. MEIGHEN I understand I was misinformed on that, but I shall give him an illustration. He has let contracts for buildings that were not in the estimates prior to 1909 all over the country, over and over again. Can he deny that?
I would be obliged to 'deny that, because there are heir* few public buildings in the estimates of this year which were not in the estimates of 1907-8.
That .would not be denying it.
He says very many; I say very few.
Would the minister give an estimate of the number?
All my hon. friend has to do is to send for the estimates of 1907 and compare them with those of this year.
The minister will not deny that there are a score?
I should doubt that very much.
The presence of one would be inconsistent with his principle in 1909 and the minister doubts that there are a score. How will the minister explain that?

It is the easiest thing in the world to do that. The words ^hich my hon. friend reads are fust what I thought, that before initiating any new works, as a general principle, the works which were provided for in the estimates of 1907-8 would be gone on with. I see how niy hon. friend fell into error. By initiating, I understand to mean the putting of an amount in the estimates for the initiation of a public building, parliament voting the money, and
