there might be exceptional cases under which we would think it desirable to proceed with some work not in the previous estimates. Then the amount would be put in and that would be the initiation of a public building. As I said before, when parliament votes money I have to treat all works alike. This corroborates entirely the statement I make. I thought the criticism was going to be that all these public works for which we are now asking votes were in the estimates of 1907-8, before the election. It will be found that 95 per cent of the items which are in the estimates to-day were in the estimates of 1907-8.

That is fust what I found fault with. I pointed out that these were pre-election pledges, and I thought it was unfair that these buildings should have precedence over others where no pre-election promise had been given, and I promply came to the conclusion that simply because these were pre-election pledges they should not have priority over other places, which had really better claims. I am sorry to hear the minister say that 95 per cent of the works he is going on with are _ for buildings proposed before the last election. I do not think the minister has made much out of the statememnt that 95 per cent of these votes are simply carrying out preelection promises.
Except to answer the hon. member for Portage la Prairie.

I would be sorry to have the minister think he had persuaded me or anybody that he had explained his own statement. He says that only 5 per cent are exceptions to the rule. That is a bad enough state of affairs as it is. There is no doubt ground for the complaint of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), but the minister is here making a solemn pledge, and unless he can show that his 5 per cent come within the exceptions he has stated he has deceived the country. He cannot show a single item of the whole 5 per cent, that he doubts amount to a score, where the need for a building was caused by flood or fire and not simply by the fact that the public building was in a constituency represented by a Liberal member.
My hon. friend says I could not show one. Time is too precious to go through them all, but let me mention Campbellton, where the public building was destroyed by fire. That is one of the new ones.
Is that the whole 5 per cent?

My hon. friend said I could not name one.
Goderich public building, addition, $8,000.
This is to make an addition to the public building at Goderich.
What is the character of the addition? -

This is to build an annex to the public building, also to make alterations to the interior fittings of the post office, as requested by the Post Office Department, and also by the Board of Trade of Goderich. The addition to the building is estimated to cost $7,023; the post office fittings, $3,000; contingencies and superintendence, $977; total estimated expenditure, $11,000. We assume that we will expend prior to 31st of March next, $2,000, and we are asking for a revote of $8,000 and that will leave $1,000 still to be provided in order to complete the work.
Harriston public building, $15,000.

Here the site has been purchased, we bought the larger portion of it from the town of Harriston. Total cost of site and expenses, $3,076; total estimated expenditure for this building will be about $20,000, not including the land. There is to be an armoury in connection with it that may increase the cost.
How much of this item for the armoury?
Possibly it may add $3,000 or $4,000 to the cost.
Is part of this expenditure to be used for the armoury?
I had asked the chief architect not to exceed $20,000; but he tells me that in consequence of the instructions to put an armoury in it, the cost may run $3,000 or $4,000 beyond that sum.
I presume I am quite in order under this item in discussing the question of drill halls generally?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Quite so.

The other day, on page 1628 of ' Hansard ', I stated that the actual cost, when the buildings were completed, ran from 25 to 75 per cent higher than the contract price; and the Minister of Public Works replied that I was entirely in error as to that. It is, then, a question of accuracy between us, and I propose to give a few facts to prove that my statement is correct. Before six o'clock I referred to one case in Nova Scotia, at Baddeck. I might also call attention to Halifax, where the contract price was $204,250, and the actual cost $279,136, or 36 per cent above the contract price. I might refer to Truro, where the contract price was $10,280, the actual cost $12,892, or 25 per cent above contract price; to which should be added, in estimating the total cost of the building, the cost of the site, which was $5,000, paid to Mr. PUGSLEY
a gentleman by the name of J. N. Pugsley, who I understand is a relative of the Minister of Public Works.
What relationship?
I said I was informed that he was a relative. If he is, I presume the hon. gentleman knows the relationship better than I do.
I have never had the pleasure of seeing or knowing that gentleman.
It is a matter, I dare say, for mutual regret for the Minister of Public Works and Mr. J. N. Pugsley ;f they are not related.
There may be a distant relationship, but I do not know what it is.

In New Brunswick I will mention Sussex: contract price, $10,523, actual cost, $14,011, or 33 per cent over contract price. Woodstock: contract price, $39,680, actual cost, $54,259, or 36 per cent over contract price. To that you may add $6,000 for the site. In Quebec, I may mention St. Hyacinthe, where the actual cost is 37 per cent above the contract price, not counting $7,500 paid for the site. In Manitoba I would refer him to Brandon, where the actual cost is 26 per cent over the contract price; and to Virden, where the actual cost is 83 per cent above the contract price. In British Columbia I might refer him to Kamloops, where the actual cost was 76 per cent above contract price; to ICaslo, where it was 85 per cent above contract price; to Rossland, where it was 45 per cent above contract price; to Revel-stoke where it was 63 per cent above contract price; and to Nelson, where the actual cost was 125 per cent above contract price. Yet the hon. gentleman told me the other day, and told this committee, that when 1 stated that the actual price averaged from 25 to 75 per cent above contract, I was entirely in error. Now I commend these figures to his consideration, and I yrant to show him that he was the gentleman who was in error and not the member for Fron-tenac.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ? I have not the figures, and many of those buildings were erected a long time before I had anything to do with the department. Is, or is not this the case, that my hon. friend first takes what he calls the contract price, which may be for the building alone, and then he adds on, to make the total cost, plumbing, heating, electric lighting, possibly sidewalks and everything of that kind, which were not in the original contract, and the cost of the site also. Is that not s j J

No, that is not the case. The main item in the contract is the price for the erection of the building. Invariably there is added to that, contracts for lighting and heating. How the cost, over and above what one would apparently think would cover everything in the construction of the building, reaches these extraordinary figures, is more than I can understand.
The details are all given.

It is a difficult matter to understand. Take, for instance, the cottages erected at Kingston. Now at that time the hon. gentleman asked for $57,000 for those buildings. The year previous he had obtained $55,000, he then adds $75,000, which made $112,000, and he estimated at that very time $96,000. Yet he obtained from this House $112,000 for buildings which his own estimate said would cost $96,000. We inquired about the details, .and why this extra money was required? That was the question which I put to him at the time the building was erected. The roof was on, the glass was in the windows, the heating apparatus was installed, the lighting fixtures were up, the walls were plastered, everything was done, yet he wanted something like $22,000 after all that had been done. I questioned the hon. gentleman in that case, and finally got him to agree to hand back $20,000 of that money. But to go on with drill halls and armouries, let me give a few instances in the province of Ontario. For Belleville drill hall, the contract price was $108,682, and the actual cost $138,511, or 27 per cent above; Brock-ville drill hall 30 per cent above the contract price; Woodstock 27 per cent above the contract price, not including the cost of the site which was $6,120; Kingston 28 per cent above, not counting the site, which cost $18,300; Hamilton 66 per cent above, not counting the site,- (which cost $6,000. That was in 1889. But let me give the history in connection with Hamilton from 1896 down. I find that the contract price was $254,276, over a quarter of a million, and that the cost was $317,937, or 25 per cent above the contract price not counting $29,000 paid for the site in 1908.
Why should my hon. friend count the site? The site is not in the contract.
I do not count it.
Then why mention it? You give the impression that the cost of the site should be added to the contract.

I will explain why I mention it. I am showing that the actual cost is very much in excess of the contract price. I merely mention the cost of the site where I give it so that any person who is interested in the total cost of the building may add the cost of the site to the final cost, not that it makes any difference in comparing the contract price with the actual cost. Dundas cost 92 per cent more; Cobourg 44 per cent and the cost of the site was $6,000; Burford 57 per cent; Brantford 92 per cent. In St. Catharines the contract was awarded for the building in October 1900, to one William Garson.
What is the percentage that the hon. gentleman gives for Cobourg?
44 per cent.
What was the contract?
I think the hon. gentleman must be wrong there. What was the actual cost?
$57,526. I think that will figure out to 44 per cent.
The hon. gentleman may be right, but that is not my information.

The contract was awarded in St. Catharines in 1900, to William Garson for $56,000. This contract was cancelled and Garson was presented with $7,288. A new contract was entered into in June, 1904, with Sullivan and Langdon for $79,829, and with others for $14,940, or a total of $94,769; in other words the contract in	1904	was 69 per centhigher than	the contract	with Mr. Garson in 1900. The total cost of this building, including the $7,288 presented to Mr. Garson, was $110,534, or 97 per cent higher than Garson's contract which was cancelled in 1900. Now, the minister, a few minutes ago said that these buildings were erected before his time. The buildings that I have referred to have been constructed since the year 1896. For the buildings under construction I may say that the contracts total up $686,906, there has been spent on them $730,744, and it is estimated that it will take $72,905 additional. That will make $803,649 to which you will have to add the cost of the sites amounting to $22,200. If you summarize this you will find the following results: Take five drill halls or armouries in the province of Nova Scotia; the contract price was $234,830, and the actual cost $312,885, or 33 per cent. Take three in New Brunswick, and they cost 32 per cent over the contract price; seven in British Columbia show an advance of 33 per cent; two in Manitoba 33 per cent; two in Quebec an advance of 23 per cent; fourteen in Ontario an advance of 27 per cent. So that, I think that I have substantiated my statement that the actual cost of drill halls or armouries erected in this country ranges from 25 to 75 per cent higher than the contract price. There are 33 buildings, the total contracts amount to $1,800,-
866, and the actual cost is $2,315,148, or an average of 28 per cent above the contract price. Then, it is interesting in connection with this matter to note that the drill halls and armouries constructed between the first of July, 1896, and December, 1909, have cost this country for construction and sites over $2,049,510. We have in Nova Scotia 166 officers and 1,812 non-commissioned officers and men making use of these buildings. If you average this cost up to see what we are paying for the whistle it means that for every officer in Nova Scotia who is making use of these buildings for drill purposes this country has paid out over $1,900 since 1896 while for each noncommissioned officer and man it cost $174. If you apply it to British Columbia the average cost per officer is $2,557 and for each non-commissioned officer and man $233 for buildings erected in that province. So, you may go through the whole lot. If you take the country over it averages nearly $2,000 for each officer and nearly $186 for each non-commissioned officer and man.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in addition to this you might put in the salaries of the engineers and firemen employed in only fifteen of these buildings and they will total $132,720 in fourteen years. The chaTge for maintenance alone from 1896 to 1908 is $76,103. We speak about the cost of militia and defence for this country. It is a matter of some $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 a year. But that is not all. You have to take in addition to that the cost of these expensive buildings, the cost of the men employed in looking after them, the cost of maintenance. Then, you have to take the millions of dollars which are being spent annually for militia and defence and put that along side the meagre, paltry sum of money which is voted by this government in the interest of agriculture. It is something that should call for strong protest from every hon. gentleman in this House. I take this opportunity of entering my protest as one member against this sort of thing. We have too much fuss and feathers. As one hon. gentleman on the other side of the House said, I think, last year we pay too much for red tape and gold braid in this country-entirely too much and I think the money, to a large extent, is worse than wasted. I think I have amply proven the assertion which I made in the House the other day, and I reiterate my argument that no dependence can be placed upon the estimates of the cost of these buildings as brought [DOT]down by the Minister of Public Works.
Invariably when the final cost of the building is ascertained we discover that the estimated cost is so entirely different from the real	fact, that there is
no reliance to be placed on the the estimates of cost presented to the committee by the minister. When the Minister of Public Works challenged the Mr. EDWARDS.
correctness of my statement that the actual cost of buildings was from 25 per cent to 75 per cent in excess of the contract price, he did not know what he was talking about, and vast as his knowledge is there is something left for him to learn. Complaint is sometimes made that the estimates are not rushed through fast enough. That is not because the members on this side desire to prevent necessary expenditure of public money, but because they have learned from bitter experience that no reliance can be placed on the figures presented by the minister, and so we have to look at all these estimates with doubt. The Minister of Public Works tells us that a certain building will cost so much and that is all it is going to cost, and he tells us of the large business interests of the locality and we feel that the country can afford to spend that much, money there, but ultimately we find that, this building costs anywhere from 25 to 75 per cent, and in one case 123 per cent, more than the contract price, which he led us to believe would be some indication as to the total cost of the building. If the architects employed by the minister do not know what they are doing let him hunt around for men who can tell somewhere near what a building is going to cost and then he will not be subject to all this criticism.

I regret that my hon. friend with all his desire to enlighten me has not succeeded further than to lead to the belief that the hon. gentleman does not measure very carefully his words. I have always found in my experience that though you may not be able at the moment to probe all the statements made by a witness, or a member of parliament either, it is a very good rule to endeavour to pick out just a few things and show the inaccuracy in regard to these, and^ then leave it to the jury or to the public, as the case may be, to judge as to what reliance may be placed in every statement made by such a witness or member. The hon. gentleman stated the other evening that drill halls and armouries generally actually cost from 25 to 75 per cent in excess of the contract price. Every one who listened to my hon. friend understood that this statement had reference to the work which was actually supposed to be included in the contract, and his argument was that through some fault of the chief architect or a desire to help the contractor, or looseness in the administration of the department, the contractor was able to draw from the public treasury from 25 to 75 per cent more than he was entitled to receive under his contract.
I made no such statement.
That is a fair inference to draw from the statement made by the hon. gentleman. He told us that the building at Baddeck cost about 35 per cent more.
Fifty-nine.

As a matter of fact the contract price for Baddeck was $2,250, and the contractor was paid to the very cent what the department had agreed to pay him by the contract without adding one cent, but the cost of the fittings for that, building was $1,500, which made the total' cost of the building, including fittings, $3,750.
What was the final cost?
And here is your own statement from your own department saying that it was $5,975. This would show that we cannot get reliable figures from your department.
That includes many other things besides the contract and the fittings.

I did not say what it included.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. No, but the hon. gentleman gave the committee to understand that through some fault of the chief architect the contractor had received from 25 to 75 per cent more than he had contracted to do the work for.

My statement wms just as clear as the English language could make it, namely that the actual price was from 25 to 75 per cent above the contract price, and that is all I said. I gave the contract price in each case as the department gave it to me, and I gave the actual cost *as the department gave it to me, and I worked out the percentage. The hon. gentleman is at liberty to draw on his imagination, as he is apt and able to do, for all the inferences he sees fit, but there are the figures. The hon. gentleman did deny the correctness of these figures but he did not speak of my drawing any inferences at that time; he wanted the committee to get the idea that the statement I made was not a fact.
Mr. PUGSLEYL I certainly do deny not only the correctness of the figures given by the hon. gentleman, but I deny the inferences he sought to draw.

They are your own figures.
Mr. PUGSLEY". The hon: gentleman repeats to-night that these buildings cost from 25 to 75 per cent more than the contract price. Does that not mean that there was a contract price for the building, and that the contract price included the fittings and the heating and the plumbing and everything else. Surely that must be the inference from his language. Take the case of a building where the contract is simply for the building of the walls and the plastering and putting in the windows and doors, and if that contract was for $40,000, and there was a contract for the fittings and the heating, and the plumbing, and the sidewalks, and electric wiring at $10,000, would it be fair to argue that the building had actually cost $10,000 more than the contract price of $40,000. Surely the cost of the fittings, heating and plumbing, and improvements of the sidewalk must all form part of the contract price; yet my hon. friend has not included them in his statement of the cost of the Baddeck armoury. The cost of the building was $2,250, and the cost of the heating $1,500, making a total of $3,750.	[DOT]
I got the figures from the hon. gentleman's department.

My hon. friend gets from my department a statement of the cost of the armoury, showing that the contract was $2,250, and sundry work, which would be the heating, $1,500, a total of $3,750. That is exactly what was agreed to be paid to the contractor. Then the hon. gentleman has added to the record of the cost all the repairs which were made to the building from year to year from 1901, when it was erected, down to the time tie got this statement, that is, for a period of nine years, and he tells this committee that that shows that this building has cost a vast percentage beyond the contract price. Does my hon. friend think that is fair?
Is that not the report from the hon. gentleman's own department?

The statement read by the hon. gentleman showed a total expenditure to date on the Baddeck armoury, including site, of $5,975.62. This return was given to the hon. gentleman on April 7. 1910, and he included in it the cost of the site and all the expenditure incurred on the building between the time the contract was let in 1901 down to 1910. Now, let us look at another; take the Cobourg armoury. I charge the hon. gentleman in that case also with adding into the expenses of construction all the expenditures for repairs on that building from year to year from 1903 down to 1910, to make a total of $57,526. Let us take another-Woodstock, Ont.; he said that had cost a very large percentage above the contract price. I charge the hon. gentleman with having done the same thing there-with having taken all the ex-

penditures in the way of repairs upon the building during a number of years after me work of construction was ended and added them to the contract price. The figures which the hon. gentleman had before him ought to have satisfied him, if he had given any care whatever to an examination of them, that the effect of his statement would be to mislead the House as to the actual cost of the building. Take Woodstock, N. B., the contract price there was $31,980, and the total amount paid $37,306-a difference of about $5,000. The hon. gentleman there also added the expenses during two years at least after the building was completed, and when work was being done which had nothing whatever to do with its construction. Later on, when the hon. gentleman's figures are printed in ' Hansard,' it may be worth while still further to expose the fallacious statement he has made and show that he is entirely mistaken with regard to the cost of these buildings.
The reason I took the liberty of differing with him the other day was that since 1 have been Minister of Public Works, I have traced with a good deal of care the cost of the different buildings erected under the supervision of the chief architect of this department, and I knew there was no such additional amount of expenditure on construction as that which was stated by the hon. gentleman. And notwithstanding the assertions which are sometimes cast by hon. gentlemen opposite and by some others on the chief architect, I desire to say-and I say it with the greatest possible pleasure-that from the experience I have had of that gentleman, I can testify to the great industry and care he always displays in the most important work of his department. He has a great deal of responsibility in connection with the erection of public buildings; and from the Observation I have had of his work, I am able to say that he does it faithfully and well. In Mr. Ewart, appointed long before this government came into power, as chief architect, the public has a most valuable servant, one who gives honest, faithful and diligent service to the country.

If I had not the opportunity of being in this committee before and of listening on many other occasions to the Minister of Public Works, I might be surprised, but I must confess that I am not one whit surprised at the argument he has just made. Last year I asked for a return with regard to public buildings, drill halls and armouries. What I asked for, was this:-
At what places in the several provinces, armouries and drill halls have been erected; the total cost of the site in each case, and' when and from whom purchased; the contract price of each building, and to whom and Mr. PUGSLEY.
when the contract was awarded; the total cost of each building; in what places armouries and drill halls are being constructed at present, and the cost of the site, from whom, when, at what price the contract was awarded, and the names of places where other armouries and drill halls are to be built by the government in the near future.
That question bears on its face its object, namely, to obtain information as to the amount of money expended on drill halls and armouries. I do not think there can be any doubt as to its meaning. When I stated the other night that the actual cost was from 25 per cent to 75 per cent in excess of the contract price, the hon. gentleman-speaking of Baddeck-said that I included in that cost all that had been expended from 1901 down to the present on the Baddeck armoury. Well, I stated precisely what the hon. gentleman himself gave me. It was from the return furnished by his own department that I took my figures. In that return which I hold in my hand, there is no detail of the expenditure at Baddeck. All it states is that the contract was awarded to Joseph Queen for $2,250, and sundry work awarded to P. H. McFarlane at $1,500.
It states a little more. It gives the total expenditure to date.
And it gives the total expenditure to date at $5,975, and that is precisely what I took into 'account.
I rise to ask a question.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister rises to ask a question, but the hon. gentleman who has the floor can refuse, if he desires.
I am going to accord to the hon. minister exactly the same courtesy which he did to me, and will ask him to wait until I get through.
That will suit me perfectly.

And suit me better. In referring to Baddeck the minister said that I included everything in this expenditure, even the site. Will he allow me to inform this committee that, according to the return furnished by his own department, the site did not cost anything, but was a free gift. I might also draw an inference from that statement of the minister. I might say that it was his intention to try and make this committee believe that I was endeavouring to include some amount for the site of the building when I had a return showing that the site cost nothing.
Take the Woodstock armoury which happens to be the next one on the list. I

included in the contract price all that was given in the return sent down by the Public Works Department. Under the heading of contractors, it says that the building was let to Williams & Fisher for $31,980; for heating apparatus, the contract was given another firm for $2,700; then there was a contract for electric wiring and fixtures $1,500. Then there was furniture and fittings $3,500. I included all these in the contract price and they brought the price up to $39,680. One would naturally think that when the contract was awarded for this building for $31,980, and when the contract was let, as shown in this return for heating apparatus, and when the contract was let for electric wiring and fixtures and fittings and furniture, you had pretty-nearly all that the building could cost when completed; and I concluded that these covered the whole contract price. I made up the amount, from the statement given in the return sent by the hon. gentleman's own department, as $39,680. And I pointed out that notwithstanding everything appeared to be covered by the contracts I have mentioned, the building cost $54,257 or 36 per cent * more than the total amount of all those various contracts I have enumerated. Could I have been fairer? Had the minister furnished me with the details of expenditures throughout these various years, I would have given them to the House; but the hon. gentleman's department furnished me with the expenditures for the different years' and they amounted to $54,257, which I gave to the House and on which I based the excess of cost over the contract price.
We all know that these large buildings are not constructed in one year. The hon. gentleman makes quite a hullabaloo about the fact that this expenditure was spread over several years. Why does the hon. gentleman do that if it is not meant by him as a herring drawn across the track to distract attention from the facts of the case? The point I endeavoured to make, and it nettled the hon. gentleman, as he showed quite clearly, was that the actual cost of these buildings was from 25 per cent to 75 per cent in excess of the contract pries. It is up to the hon. gentleman, if he is not satisfied with that, if he wants to draw inferences, and if he thinks the House draws inferences from that, to make it clear where the rest of the money went. It is not up to me. I take the return as provided by him. It is up to him to draw inferences, and to explain them to the House and to the country. There is a feeling in the country that these buildings are costing much more than they should, that men are given a contract on a building and that_'extras are thrown in before the building is completed to the extent of thousands of dollars. In the neighbourhood of Kingston we have a clear instance of this in connection with the construction of cottages for soldiers. After everything was completed the hon. gentleman asked this committee for $20,000 more than was required to complete the building, when even the glass and fixtures were in and it was only after drumming that point at him that he consented to give the $20,000 back, to reduce the vote, and now he tries to distract attention from the real point I am making by implying that I am throwing out insinuations. I am not dealing in hi* sinuations to-night, but in figures furnished by the hon. gentleman's department, and it is up to the hon. gentleman to explain what inference is to be drawn from this sort of thing. The same thing applies to Woodstock, N.B., and Cobourg. He found fault with my statement in regard to Cobourg. That expenditure I gave, also, from the statement furnished me by the_ hon. gentleman's department. I included in the contract, which was for $35,550, also the contract for fittings, $4,395, making the total contract, which I had a right to suppose, from the documents furnished me by the hon. gentleman's department, amounted to $35,945.	1 take the hon. gentleman s
own statement in regard to the expenditure of 1902 to 1909, for various amounts paid as the building progressed, and it appears to be $57,526.25. I repeat that it is not up to me to explain the details; I have not the information to explain them. If the non. gentleman sees fit to draw on his imagination for inferences and to conclude that the people of this country think that these buildings are costing from 25 per cent to 75 per cent more than the contract price, and that the money might be spent more carefully, it is up to him to explain it. The inference does exist in the public mind, and the public are not satisfied with the way he handles their money. It is all very wrell for the minister to undertake to twist a man's statement, but in this case he is occupying the unique position of endeavouring to twist and distort a statement furnished by his own department in answer to an order of this House. We all know how able and capable the hon. gentleman is in turning around a corner, but it has kept him busy this evening to twist around and get on both sides of this question.

What I charge against the hon. gentleman, and what I reaffirm against him is that, having in his possession a return furnished by tlie Department of Public Works, which gave on its face the total expenditure to date down to 1910, when that return was asked for, he did not inform the committee that the figures he gave included all repairs and expenses of every kind and description, which had been made on these buildings subsequent to the completion of the contract. That is the

charge I made, that is the charge I repeat, and that is the charge from which the hon. gentleman cannot escape. There is no question about that. When the hon. gentleman says that this department gave him a return, so it did, but what did it profess to give on its face? It gave the total cost incurred in connection frith the building to date. The hon. gentleman has been here long enough to know that when I am asked in regard to public buildings, as, for instance, a day or two ago in regard to the post office building at Montreal, the total cost to date, I gave the cost from the construction of the building 40 or 50 years ago, not only during the time of construction, but down to the very time when my memoranda were made up in 1911. My hon. friend has been here long enough to know, he must have known, that such a return gives not only the cost of construction, the contract price, the fittings, heating, cost of site, all repairs to the building right from the very first down to the present time, whether it is 5, 10, 20 or 50 years. My hon. friend ought to have known that the figures he has given as to the total cost of the work, which he say.s exceeded the estimate bv 25 per cent to 75 per cent, included all these items.
I beg pardon.
They do, whenever the site has been paid for, they do.
I beg pardon, they do not.
I say they do. That return gives the total expenditure upon the buildings to date.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say I included the cost in my percentage.
Did not the hon. gentleman give the total expenditure to data from that statement?.
I did not include the cost of site.
The site is included in every case.
I did not include the cost of site.
Did the hon. gentleman deduct the cost of site?
I certainly did not.
Let me take the case of Woodstock, N.B.
What is the cost of the site there?

It is not a question of what difference it makes, because in either case it might be $6,000. What I charge against the hon. gentleman is that he had Mr. PUGSLEY.
in his possession a return made by the department, showing the total expenditure to date, which the hon. gentleman either knew or ought to have known includes every item of cost of every kind or description, from the time the survey of the site was undertaken, including advertising, including legal expenses, including contract price, including fittings, heating, plumbing, electric wiring, sidewalks, any sewerage there might be, and all repairs from the day when the construction was completed right down to the time when the return was moved for ; and, the hon. gentleman sought to lead the committee to believe that that represented the cost of the building which was supposed to have been included in the original contract price. That is the charge which I make against the hon. gentleman, and that is the charge from which he cannot escape. Now, take the case of Woodstock. The hon. gentleman gave the total cost as $73,091.78, yet the hon. gentleman had before him a statement showing the expenditure beginning with the year 1902 running down to the year 1909, and I say that included, as the hon. gentleman ought to know, the survey of the site, the cost of the site, the legal expenses, the advertising, the contract price for the building, the fittings, heating, plumbing, electric wiring, sidewalks and all repairs which were made subsequent to the time the construction was finished down to the very day the return was moved for. But, the hon. gentleman sought to make this committee believe that this amount of $73,091 represented the cost which ought to have been included, and which was supposed to have been included, in the original contract price for the building.

If there is anything misleading in it, the parties who are responsible for it are those who furnished the return to this House. It does not appear, so far as I could learn on the face of the paper, thatNthere were repairs included in that from time to time. We know for a fact that the erection of these buildings extends, over many years. While I have been in the House I have watched the progress of the erection of buildings year after year. After the buildings are commenced it is sometimes three, or four or five, six or seven years before they are finished. The answer given to the hon. member's question including the contract price and cost of building complete, does not say down to what date.
It does say to this date.

That return was furnished by the minister's department and by his orders ; then I say that he above all others is responsible for misleading the

House and the country, if there is anything to mislead in the statement that has been furnished here. My hon. friend only read out the return as given to him, and if the returns -which we got are not reliable, then it behooves the Minister of Public Works to be more careful in what he presents to this House.

My hon. friend from Frontenac ought to be very thankful to my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) for trying to strengthen the defence he has endeavoured to make against the charge I have brought against him, and successfully, I think. The hon, gentleman says that the department is responsible. What would the hon. gentleman think if I were to assure him, as I have already assured the committee, that that return gives the figures showing the expenditure year after year, and shows the total expenditure down to the year 1910, when that return was moved for. It includes the cost of thh site. The site in every case is included in these figures, and the hon. gentleman put that in and added it to the total figures, by which means he sought to make a comparison against the original contract price.

Unfortunately for the argument of the Minister of Public Works in most of the cases which 'he saw fit to cite, the site did not cost anything. However, in comprising the total expenditure with the contract price, I took the figures furnished by the hon. gentleman's department, and proved what I stated the other day, that the actual cost was some 25 to 75 per cent in excess of the contract price. In the return thus furnished to me, in at least two-thirds of the instances which I gave this evening, the site cost nothing ; so that part of the hon. gentleman's argument falls entirely to the ground.

Taking the first item, Baddeck harbour :	The contract
price is apparently, $2,250, sundry work, $1,550, making $3,800. Taking that from the total expenditure, leaves $2,225. What would that be for?

That could be arrived at by looking at the Public Accounts. I am not supposed to have that information with me. But that includes the total expenditure, the survey of the site, the legal expenses, advertising, salary of the clerk of works, travelling expenses, contingencies, repairs, everything right down to date.
Does the hon. gen-tie-man think these small items would amount to the contract price of the armoury itself?

Yes, running over that number of years.
Kingston post office, addition to building and alterations, $25,000.

This is for the purpose of making a two story addition to the building, 55 x 35 feet ; also to make alterations in the interior fittings, &c. The total estimated cost of $25,000. Additional accommodation is considered by the Post Office Department to be urgently required.
I would like to ask the minister why no work was done on this building last year although an appropriation was made for the work?
We did not reach it in the ordinary course last year. The plans have now been approved by the Post Office Department and it is proposed to go on with the work as speedily as we can.
You must have reached it in some way because there was an expenditure of $2,000. What was that for?
That is the estimated expenditure up to the 31st March next. >
I notice that there was a vote for this some years ago of $7,785, while the expenditure is only going on now.

They have been getting along as well as they could.
Kingston Royal Military College, covered drill hall, $15,000.
The word ' covered ' is a misprint and it should be struck out.
Is this a new building or an addition?
A new building.
When did it first appear in the estimates?
It was in last year and I am inclined to think that it was in pre-, viously.
It is a drill hall?

Yes, a drill hall for
the cadets.
I think I can advise the minister that it was not in previously. I have the proceedings for 1908. Would the minister kindly explain if the old drill hall was burned down or carried away by a flood?	_
No. I may say that I am. substituting this for a building which did appear. There was a skating rink which appeared and I decided to drop that item and put this drill hall in for the cadets.

I have the estimates for 1908 and I will read the Kingston items* for the information of the minister :



Kingston Koyal Military College, new quarters, additional amount.
Kingston post office, addition to building and alterations to fittings.
Kingston military buildings, repairs and renewals to blocks A, C and E, Tete du Pont barracks, &c., inclusive of electric ligthing, &c.
That is all the Kingston buildings. I do not know which of these items relates to this vote.
This was in last year at all events.

It is being gone ahead with contrary to the pledge the minister gave in 1909, and it does not come within the exception of fire or flood. Will the minister explain why this is being gone ahead with in preference to buijdings that were in the estimates for 1908?

We had some items for the year 1907-8, I am quite sure. I do not profess to keep all these things in my head, but my recollection is that we dropped some two or three items for Kingston which did not seem to be quite so urgent as this drill hall and we put in an amount for the drill hall. This seems to be very urgent. Kingston Military College is doing a splendid work_ for the young men of the country, this is urged by the college authorities and we do not think that we ought to postpone any longer in providing for it.

I am afraid the minister is not very accurate. All that vote in the 1908 estimates appears since as being pursued. I see nothing dropped. Is the minister going to assert that all that is necessary to any one of those later items is simply to assure the committee that they appear to be very urgent and consequently he has decided to go on ? If so, the pledge which he made in 1909 was just so much chaff and straw.
If they were urgent and parliament voted the money last year why did he not spend it ?

There is another question that I would like to put to the minister in connection with this building. 1 notice that the item is for $15,000. I will not be very certain that I am correct, but I think I am correct in saying that we were informed earlier in the session that any militia buildings, the cost of which was not to exceed $15,000, were sujtposed to come under the supervision in their construction of the Minister of Militia; that is, that the Minister of Militia was supposed to be capable of looking after the construction of a building that did not cost more than $15,000.
The estimated cost is $29,000.

Of course, that puts it beyond the intellectual powers, I suppose, of the Minister of Militia. We have to assume then that he is only capable of looking after the construction of a building that does not cost more than $15,000, but when the cost exceeds $15,000 it requires^ a person of the mental calibre of the Minister of Public Works to look after it. In that case, there are many buildings which, in my opinion, might be constructed for $14,000 or $15,000 which will cost a little more than that, so that the Minister of Public Works will get the handling of them.
Kingston Royal Military College, additional dormitory accommodation for cadets, $30,000.
Is this a new building?

It is a new building. My hon. friend no doubt, has heard of the demand for this. I visited the Royal Military College, I saw the officer in command and he called my special attention to the necessity for another dormitory for the students of the college. He said that they needed that perhaps more than anything else in connection with the college buildings.
How many cadets are in attendance at that institution ?
I understand the minister to say that this is also a new building ?
Yes.
Was it in the 1908 estimates ?
Yes.
That is two.
What is this building to cost when it is completed ?
The estimated cost is $75,000.
The contract is not let ?
Not yet.
Are the plans out ?
They are not ready yet.
I presume it will be let. by contract ?
Yes.
Where have the students, been sleeping previous to this time-out in. the air ?

There is a dormitory, and it was first thought that we might provide the requisite accommodation by put;

ting an additional roof on the existing dormitory, but the militia authorities, or Lt.-Col. Crowe, the commander, strongly urged the erection of a new building, stating that to put an additional story on the present one, would not afford the accommodation which it is desirable and absolutely necessary to give the students.
When was that building erected and how much did it cost ?
It is a very old building erected by the Imperial government.
What has become of it, or what use is going to be made of it ?
It is there still.
I did not suppose that it would move away. What use is it going to be put to ?
It will still be used as a dormitory because I do not imagine the new building will give all the accommodation that is needed and I presume that they will still use the old one.
Has the number of cadets been increasing from year to year?

It is so .represented. There are 104 at present. If they had additional accommodation they would get more students. It is stated they are absolutely without the accommodation necessary for the comfort of the students.
If you accommodated 104 students last year and there is no increase this year why do you require such a large expenditure as this?
They are not able to accommodate many of the applicants.
Have they accommodation for an extra number now in the buildings other than the dormitory?
I think so.
We are to spend $78,000 to accommodate an additional number of students and there is no one to tell us where that additional number is to come from.

The Militia Department,
through Lieutenant Colonel Crowe, asks for accommodation for 100 cadets additional. I do not know how many additional students they would be likely to have immediately, but my information is that if the accommodation were provided the number would rapidly increase. The Kingston Military College is exceedingly popular among the people of this country and it has turned out a great many good citizens who have taken high positions in Canada and in all parts of the world.

I have heard from time to time criticisms of the Kingston Military
College. There are times when it is popular and times when it is unpopular.
I do not think you hear much criticism now.

I do not say that the Royal Military College does not give a good education and turn out very good men, but there is an opinion in the country that everything connected with that military college is very expensive and that a great deal of what transpires there is nonsensical. There is a strong feeling in the country that a great deal of the money we invest there is wasted or worse than wasted.
We are told that the estimated cost of this dormitory is to be $75,000, and our experience would lead us to believe that the cost will be $100,000 when we get through with it.
I do not see why you should think that.

The minister tells us that the building is to accommodate 100 additional students, and if that be so then we are to spend $1,000 per sleeping room per student. Some short time ago we erected sixteen little houses there at a cost of $7,000 a house, for the accommodation of labouring men who were receiving $25 a month in actual cash pay and some perquisites which brought their pay to perhaps $40 a month. The gross rental is supposed to bring about 10 per cent of the cost of a building, and here we are providing houses worth in rental $700 a year for men whose pay all told is about $500 a year. I have had acquaintance with Kingston for a great many years and I speak of what I know when I say that there were buildings there down near the water for the accommodation of these men, which we tore down and erected these new ones, and the old buildings were much better than the average man in Canada is living in to-day. It seems to me that in this case it would strike the people of Canada as very extraordinary that we should pay $1,000 each for sleeping apartments for 100 students.
In what way are we interested in these students of the Military College?

My hon. friend can hardly expect me to reply to that, when for a great many years both parties in this country have recognized that the Kingston Military College is an institution which it was desirable in the first place to establish and afterwards to maintain in a state of efficiency. In this college our young men receive a military training and also a training in engineering which is of the very highest value to them and to the country also. In this country, which is developing Tapidly, where important public works are being undertaken, it is most desirable to

have coming out from year to year a number of young men who are thoroughly trained in engineering work. However, I am not here to-night to advocate the desirability of establishing the college. It has been established and has been maintained from time to time by both political parties. All will agree that if it is desirable-to have the college, it is desirable to afford the requisite accommodation for the youth being educated there.

That does not answer the question I asked. I understand that there are 104 students there now, and I want to know if this building is to be erected to provide accommodation for another hundred students. I quite understand that the institution is for the purpose of educating young men as civil or mechanical engineers. If it is, there are many other places where it is possible for young men to get that education. I understood the minister to say that these young men were making good in other parts of the world. I do not see why we should be training young men to go to other parts of the world unless we want to get rid of them. There is a very strong demand for post office buildings all through this country, and the $100,000 which is the estimated cost of this building, would provide many post office buildings in towns and villages throughout the country where they are much needed.- You will find very few of these Kingston military college men among the officers of the standing army which we have in Canada. In most cases they send across the water for officers. I would like to ask why the Minister of Militia, who would be particularly interested in this building, is not here to explain the necessity for it if there is any. Has the hon. Minister of Public Works any idea why he is not here and where he is? .

I do not know personally, but I saw by the papers that he was at his home in Nova Scotia. If my hon. friend, or any other hon. gentleman desires the Kingston items to stand, I am quite willing to let them stand until the Minister of Militia is here.

I noticed that the Minister of Militia was attending a public meeting on the 18th of this month in Kings* county, assisting to elect his friend, Mr. Wickwire, to the local legislature. I think the position he occupies demands his attendance here and not in Nova Scotia trying to elect a man whom the people refused to elect a short time ago. I would like to ask him how long it takes at Kingston to fit a man to be sent out equipped with spurs and feathers. As the Minister of Militia would rather be in Nova Scotia helping in the elections, I -would sav, let him stay there, we can do very well without him, Mr. PUGSLEY.
and let us strike out this item and use the money in building post offices in a number of towns and villages throughout the Dominion which are entitled to them.
As the Minister of Militia is not here, we will pass over the Kingston items.
I would like in the meantime to get some information. Is this to be a separate building or to be attached to some other building?
It will be a separate building.
Of what material will it be constructed?
A brick building with stone finish.
Have the plans been prepared?
Not yet.
What will be the size of the building?
About 130 feet in length, 96 feet in front, and two wings each 35 feet wide at the rear.
How many stories ?
Three stories at least, besides the basement.
Is there any limit now as to' the number of students who w'ill be taken into the college?

The accommodation is so limited that they cannot take any more at present. That is the reason given by the department for this new dormitory, which will give accommodation for 100 additional students.
Has there been a rule in force restricting the number of students tr one hundred?
No, except that the accommodation is not sufficient for more than 100-that is, sleeping accommodation.
Is there not a restriction as to the number of students taken in the college each year?
Of course, being unable to accommodate more than 100, they would have to refuse applications.
Does the minister know, of his personal knowledge, that such is the reason why they refuse more students?
No, I do not, of my own knowledge, but that is -what I am informed.

I understand there is a restriction for other reasons. I under-

stand that a student can go to that college and be 'educated in the profession of a civil engineer without any reference whatever to his being adapted or required for military purposes thereafter. I understand that each student is given his education in that college regardless altogether of his services being made use of afterwards from a military standpoint.

I would not undertake to give information as to the military side of the college. Does not my hon. friend think that when I have said I would let the item stand until the Minister of Militia could be here, it would be better to await his coming before asking these questions?
If the hon. minister will answer those questions, we might let the item pass.
I might give erroneous information. My information would only be hearsay.

I understand that a student in that college .graduates as a civil engineer, and then, when he leaves the military college, he is under no obligation to serve the state as a military man? If that be the case, I do not know that we are justified spending money for that purpose, especially under the head of a military building. Personally, I do not think I would be justified in voting for this resolution. As the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has said, this seems to be a vpry exorbitant sum that we are going to pay. It amounts to $1,000 per Joed for sleeping accommodation for the 100 students who go to that college, many of whom do not go there for the military training, and. for the purpose of serving the state in a military capacity, but simply to receive an education which will enable them to earn a livelihood in other professions. Does the $75,000 include furniture, fittings, electric lighting, or heating-
The $75,000 is estimated to include everything. I have not a detailed estimate, but that is what the chief architect tells me.
I suppose the government own the site?
Yes.

From our experience in the past of the actual cost of public buildings, especially at Kingston, as compared with the estimated cost, we are justified in saying that this will probably cost $100,000, or $1,000 per student. What guarantee have we that, even if we put up this building, the 100 extra students which it will accommodate will apply to be accommodated? Has the minister any assurance to that effect?
No, I have nothing beyond the request for the building.
The request from whom?
From the commanding officer, Lf.-Col. Crowe.

At the instance, probably, of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty).
Mr. PUGSLEY\ No, I have not heard from him at all.
I think we are not justified in voting that amount for that purpose. I therefore move that the item be struck out.
Let the item stand.

If I may offer a few words in explanation, I can give some information regarding the position of the college and the necessity for the building now under consideration, and the committee may then have a little better knowledge of the situation than at present. I have been slow to take any part in the discussion for the simple reason that while the college is called the Kingston Military College, as a matter of fact it is not in Kingston. It is situated in the riding of Frontenac, and I presume that the information which has been asked by various members might very properly have been furnished by the hon. member for that riding (Mr. Edwards) did he see fit to give it, rather than bv myself, who represents a riding which is barely adjoining that in which this college is situated. The college, being in the county of Frontenac, in the village across the bay from Kingston, is usually known by the name of the Kingston Military College, no doubt from the fact of its being close to the city, which is much larger than the village of Barriefield, some three miles away, where it really is. The situation regarding the building is this: The wing which has been in use as a dormitory ever since the college was opened, was built by the Imperial government long years ago, and the late Alexander McKenzie was foreman of its construction. That building has been in use as a dormitory ever since the college was opened. For the past four or five years every room, which should be occupied by a single student or cadet, instead qf being used only by one, has to accommodate two or three, and I believe, in some few instances, four. This made it necessary for the Commandant of the institution to ask the government to provide an additional building to be used as a dormitory, so that every cadet could be housed and cared for in a room of his own. Whether that is advisable or not is a question for the House to determine, and it is not for me to offer any opinion upon it. Regarding the ques-

The hon. member misquoted me altogether. I did not speak with regard to the doing away with the military college at Kingston, I simply spoke of the effect of making additions; of going on increasing militarism in Canada when I thought that we required the money for something else. If I indicated anything else I did not intend to do so.
Perhaps I misunderstood you.

So far as the naval college in my own city is concerned, I think it is something like the college in Kingston, it is a college with nothing for the people to do after they get through it. We have a naval college but no navy up to the present day, and there does not seem to be much hope of getting one either under present conditions. I do not propose to discuss that question, the people in Halifax are prepared to deal with it and we have already put ourselves on record in regard to it. I have put myself on record in regard to the naval college and the navy and I feel something the same about that, as about the extension of the college at Kingston. If there is an estimate in this book that should be struck out, it is this very estimate that we are on now and I am quite prepared to vote that it be struck out. The Minister of Public Works tells us he cannot build a post offioe here or there, although requisitions have been in for years and years, and members on both sides have requested public buildings, yet we find that money is being thrown into an institution which the Minister of Public Works tells us is turning out engineers. There are other colleges in Canada turning out engineers, both civil and mechanical, and why should we set ourselves up in competition with these colleges all over the Dominion, which we are so glad to have. The military college has 104 students and we are now prepared to extend it and make room for another 100.
I wonder what the farmers and other electors will think of this. If we go on spending $100,000 every two or four years on this college, we will soon have more fuss and feathers in Canada than anything else. That is not what I am here for. I am here

to try and do the best I can for the people of Canada and not to go on constructing additions to the military college at Kingston. I have every desire and wish that this item should be struck out of the estimates.
Item allowed to stand.
Listowel public building, $18,000.

This is to provide for the erection of a public building in Listo-we'l. The population was 2,693, nine years ago. It is growing well, the revenue from the post office is $6,000 odd, $30,000 were paid for money orders issued and $25,000 paid. The plans are now being prepared.
This is another example of what I spoke of, either loading up the estimates with items that it is not intended to go on with, or that are not needed.

There has been no unnecessary delay. An order in council was passed in March, 1909, to purchase a site. In the ordinary course we had to prepare plans and there is a vast deal of work in the department, hon. gentlemen do not realize how much. The architects are constantly at work and are doing the best they can. There has been no unnecessary delay.
What is done by the department after the plans are prepared and entirely approved of by the other departments concerned ?	,
The specifications are sent to the Printing Bureau and advertisements issued calling for tenders.
How long does it take the Printing Bureau to print the specifications ?
It depends on how busy they are, sometimes three weeks, sometimes four, sometimes longer.

In 1909-10 there was $15,000 put in for 1911. It says $1,100 lapsed. That is not put in the column where revotes of an estimate voted the previous year, that is 1909, are put. Therefore, it must have been at least 1908 or 1907' that this was voted. Now, I presume that an application has been made for a building, that the government reached the conclusion that a building was needed there. They asked for a vote in 1906, or 1907, or 1908. They got a vote of $1,100 for some purpose, presumably for buying a site, but nothing is done with it. That has been carried on up to the present time, and now we are providing for 1912. This same item, therefore, must have been under consideration for three or four years. Either the building was needed or it was not needed. If it was
needed, and that conclusion was reached by the House, then the building should have been erected.
If we get the plans and specifications prepared, we may let the contract before the 31st of March this year. We can let it on the vote of last year.

Why didn't you let it
before?

Because we did not get ready.
Midland public building, $10,000.
This is to provide a public building for a post office and customs purposes.

The minister will admit that this is another building that was not provided for at all in the 1908 estimates. What explanation has the minister to offer for urgency, except that the constituency is represented by a Liberal?

The explanation is that a public building is much required in Midland. Midland has been growing very rapidly of recent years, and it has outgrown altogether the present accommodation, which is in a rented building. The revenue last year was $9,000, while the customs duties were $56,734. Money orders issued were $59,556 ; money orders paid, $23,654. Value of exports, $341,000 last year ; imports, $1,065,528 ; goods entered for consumption, $1,121,561. Midland is forging ahead with wonderful rapidity. It has a great blast furnace, it is doing a very large shipping business, it has extensive coal docks, a large number of lumber mills. It would be simply a crying shame to leave Midland any longer without a public building. That is why I have made an exception to the rule, and am providing a new item for a public building at Midland.

That of course will always be the explanation. Now the minister knows as well as I do that that absolutely is not contemplated by him in his statement made on page 1300 of the ' Hansard.' If that kind of explanation is to be accepted, that the town is thriving and the accommodation is inadequate, then the minister's statement meant nothing, and he knows it. The cases he gave were these, there might be others, but they would need to be of the same character, that is to say, there may be cases such as a public building being burned down, or a wharf carried away, which might create an exception. Now that may have been all the minister thought of, but if the statement meant anything, it meant that there would be no exception except such as those given, not

because representations had been made that the town was growing, that there were blast furnaces in it, that the revenue of the post office was increasing, that the citizens asked _ for it. That can be said anywhere you like. Now the minister must know that his statement meant nothing at all, if he is allowed to get out of it by the explanation he offers now. But I tell the minister that the people of this country at the time placed some reliance upon it, and I hope he has not got past the point when he is at least anxious that this committee will take him at his word.

I have only to say this, that absolute good faith is being kept with the various cities and towns of this country in respect to which provision was made in the estimates of 1907-8. Have we left out any of these? Not one, except where further inquiry satisfied us the building was not needed in the public interest. We are carrying everything out in good faith. What does my hon. friend complain of? Does he complain because we are going to erect a public building at Midland, having the revenue at out disposal? Does he mean that we shall not go on with a public building in Midland, when we are not interfering with the erection of a public building anywhere else? I cannot understand what he is complaining of, what he is grumbling about. How am I guilty of bad faith? Surely I have a perfect right, when I am providing for these other buildings, to have regard to the necessities of people in other sections of the country, and to submit to my colleagues an amount for other public buildings. If my hon. friend means to say that a public building is not as much required in Midland as a public building at Portage la Prairie, or some other place, let him say it. But he knows that Midland is as much entitled to a public building as the town from which he comes, if not more.

I am not comparing the necessities of Midland with the necessities of Portage la Prairie, and the minister knew I was not. I wanted to know whether the minister meant what he said when he uttered the works spoken on page 1300. I do not know anything about Midland. But what I am complaining of is this : The minister says the word ' initiate ' means asking parliament for a vote. Now, if it means that, he is violating his word given to this committee on page 1300. He says he should not be debarred from going ahead in other places. He told the House that his department is overworked. What is it that overworks his department? The placing of estimates before the committee, the preparing of plans and specifications to get ready to go on with the work. Now, he gave this committee his word that he would not overwork his department in order that he
might go ahead with other work. We relied upon that. It has not been carried out. That is what I complain of.

The minister gives as a reason why he goes on with this building that there is urgent need for it because Midland is a growing place. That very same argument could and would have applied with equal force at any time during the last ten years. Midland has been an active, growing place for ten years, and the need was as great six or seven years ago as now. But there i3 a strange coincidence in the fact that the proposal is made now when Midland or the constituency in which it is situated, is represented in this House by a friend of the government, whereas, up to the last parliament, it was not. That seems to be the explanation of it.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to object to the item?

No, I am not objecting to the item, but I am objecting to the argument which the minister advances as justifying the item. We find this very same condition of things in other counties as well. Take the county of Wellington, if you like. There are two post offices that we have voted money for to-night within three miles of each other. Two more post offices are being built in that same county. Another is hardly finished yet, making five in the one county that happens to be represented in this House by supporters of the government. Go to the adjoining counties, and how many do you find? In many of them not one government building. Midland was needing a post office for years, but so long as it was represented by a member of the opposition, in the judgment of the minister, and his friends there was no necessity for a post office. No money could be voted for it and none was asked. But, it turned out entirely different when they managed to get a supporter in this House from that riding. That, I take it, is a more correct argument in very many of these cases.
If a public building is needed my hon. friend ought to be glad that we are at last acceding to the wishes of the people.
I am not objecting to it at all, but I am objecting to the argument that the minister advances in support of it.
The item is all right although the argument may not be good.

Touching upon the same point brought forward by my hon. friend from Grey, that is the explanation of all this change, the minister told us a little while ago that 95 per cent of the esti-

214G
mates for this year were in the 1907-8 estimates leaving only 5 per cent for new buildings. I have gone through the list of new buildings in Ontario, there are thirty, as I make it, and eight were not in the 1907-8 estimates. But the most remarkable fact of all is that the whole eight are in constituencies represented by supporters of the government. Surely the thing is too transparent to last any longer. Surely the minister sees that it is utterly impossible to convince any sensible person that he is not making his department a party, political tool. If the minister wishes me to give the list of the eight I am ready to do so.
I am not anxious.
I do not wonder that the minister is not anxious.
I don't want to waste time.

It seems to me we have no sufficient information respecting this $10,000 to justify our consenting to its passage. How much information have we so far? We have been told that it is proposed to erect a public building in Midland, and that Midland is a thriving town. That is not sufficient.
You have the population, the postal revenue and the customs revenue.
Did the minister give the population ?
I gave all that.

Then it is my fault that I did not hear it. But, there are several other items of information. We are asked for $10,000. None of us understands that $10,000 is asked for the building. We are not told whether it is to be a mere post office or a customs house, or whether it is a combined post office and customs house, whether it is to cost $50,000 or $100,000, whether it is to be built of wood, or brick or stone, or what the dimensions of it are. We are not told even what the minister proposes to do with this $10,000. If the minister, when he approaches one of these items, would make a full and frank statement of the conditions in the town concerned, the necessity for the building, what the government are paying now for the use of a building so as to show whether it would be advantageous to the country, instead of continuing to rent, to erect a new building, setting forth the necessities for it, the amount of money that he proposes to spend, the dimensions of the building that he proposes to erect, whether it is to be for a post office or a post office and customs house, presenting a frank statement of that kind, I fancy, instead of waiting until two or three members of the opposition shy questions at him that he would get these items through much more expeditiously. Perhaps the minister would give us some more information of the kind that I have indicated now, and if he will, as far as I am concerned, I will assist the passage of this item.

I should be very glad indeed, if it would do what the hon. gentleman believes it would. Hon. gentlemen opposite ask questions for the sake of getting information. They would not like me to give all the information voluntarily, because it would leave them with nothing to question me about. They might think that I was taking too much time just as in the case of Chesley. I had just begun to explain a few of these things when hon. gentlemen called out ' carried ' because it happened to be in a constituency represented by a member of the opposition. They might cry out with equal impatience if 1 were to go into details with regard to constituencies represented by my friends. In the case of Midland, I gave all the information which any reasonable man would require. I stated that Midland was a rapidly growing place, I stated the postal revenue, I stated the customs revenue, the imports and the exports which are very large, I stated that there was a great necessity for a public building, I referred to the different industries and I was ready to answer any question that any hon. gentleman would put to me. The population nine years ago was upwards of 3,000, and I suppose it is 5,000 or 6,000 to-day. With regard to the $10,000, we propose to use. that for the purpose of buying the site, and with regard to the cost, we propose to erect a good, substantial building which will be a credit to the town and the country and we hope that it will not exceed $35,000. We intend to use it for post office and customs purposes.

Have you any offer for a site ?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. No, there were some negotiations.
Mitchell publio building, $18,000.

This is to provide for the erection of a public building at Mitchell. The site has been purchased, plans and specifications are prepared and we are now ready to advertise, which we expect to do in the course of a very few days. The population nine years ago was close on 2,000 the revenue last year was $4,079, customs duties. $96,689, money orders issued $25,540 and money orders paid $15,240. Mitchell is a thriving town in South Perth.
There was an expenditure last year of $2,000 on this.
The site was bought from the municipal corporation for $1,600, and we expect to spend $2,000 by the 31st of March.
What is the building to cost?
From $20,000 to $25,000. It is for a post office, custom house, inland revenue and armoury for B Company of the Perth Regiment.
Then a portion of the cost should be charged to the Militia Department.
We do not charge anything to the Militia Department for armouries.

You ought to, or your bookkeeping is fallacious. When we ask for a return giving the expenditure on Militia and Defence, are we to understand that the cost of such an armoury as this would not be charged to the Militia Department?	.
If a return showing the cost of armouries were brought down I should think that the proportionate cost of such a building as this devoted to military purposes ought to be properly included.
It should be charged to Militia in the public accounts, or else the public accounts are wrong.
We erect custom houses and post offices and do not charge them to these departments.
Yes, but you keep a separate account for expenditure on Militia and Defence, and unless such a cost as this were included the expenditure would not be correctly represented.

It is worthy the consideration of the Minister of Finance as to whether a proportion of the cost of such an armoury as this might not be included in the account for armouries. I will mention the matter to the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Finance, and see what they think about it.
Is Mitchell one of these thriving, growing towns we have heard so much of to-night?
Mitchell is a thriving town.
What is the population?
Nine years ago it was 1,945.
What is the population now?
I would have to ask the Chairman as to that.
If I thought that was a subject of legitimate inquiry from the Chairman I would ask him myself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I will have to decline to answer any questions when I am in the chair, but if it is the desire to have information which I only possess I shall leave the chair and ask another hon. member to take my place.
I' Tealize that very fully, and that is why I did not ask you.

As the Chairman is the only one I thought able to give the information with accuracy, I thought I would refer to the matter in an undertone, which is different from addressing Mr. Chairman across the floor. I do not know the population of any of these towns from year to year, but my information is that Mitchell is quite a thriving place
Will the minister give the source of his information?
What difference does it make? Is not this trifling with the time of the House?

The files in my department say that Mitchell is a progressive town surrounded by a thriving agricultural country, that it is a station on the Grand Trunks railway, has four churches, thirty stores, four hotels, five mills, two banks, two newspaper offices.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am now quite prepared to give any information that may be asked with regard to Mitchell, which is in the riding I represent. When the item was last before the committee I told the committee that Mitchell is a thriving town like I think every other town in western Ontario. It is improving in its general appearance, in the wealth of its people, in the buildings it possesses, rather than in population. Mitchell is in the centre of an excellent agricultural country as are all the towns in Ontario, west of Toronto. It supplies an unusually large district with its mail matter, as I know from having sent to my constituents letters in much larger numbers to that town than to other towns in proportion to its size. The- present post office is in a small crumbling building. I have had occasion to go into it on some wet days about the time of the distribution of the mail, and I can assure you I left as rapidly as possible. The town has needed a new post office very badly for some time. At the time the town itself requested a post office, there was no available building, as the shops were all filled in the business street. The desire for a public building was manifested by the people themselves. It is usually thought that the request for a public building comes from the member

for the riding, but in this case I will be telling you the absolute truth when I say that when I was informed that the board of trade and the council of that town were moving in the matter, and had requested a public building, I regretted the fact. Not that I thought Mitchell was not entitled to a public building, when taken in comparison with very many such towns that had such buildings, but I realized that just such a situation as this would arise, when it is not very pleasant to have to explain the particular demands of your own place and have it compared with others that perhaps feel just as keenly they should have a public building, and may perhaps be able to show on the face of it better reason for having a public building. I realize that Mitchell is no larger than some other towns that have not public buildings, but when I consider that the present office is quite inadequate and even unwholesome for the officials who have to be there, and that it was not possible for the department or the postmaster to find a suitable building, and that the town was so interested as to offer a portion of its market square for the new building, I think I was justified in doing what I did, not on my own initiative or that of the town, but in reply to a letter from the department asking what my opinion was-expressing the opinion, as I did, that under the circumstances the town of Mitchell was entitled to a new building at a reasonable cost.

In order that I may not
be misinterpreted, I wish to say that I was anxious that the accuracy of the minister's information as to all these towns should be put to any test that I was able to bring to bear. I have no doubt that what the hon. member who represents South Perth says is correct, in so far as it is a presentation of the facts. I make no statement as to the relative merits of Mitchell and other places; I do not know enough about it for that; but I think I do know enough about it to say, what the hon. member refrained from contradicting, that Mitchell, instead of growing and on that account deserving consideration, is on the down grade so far as population is concerned. I only wish, if the minister's inspiration has been the member for the riding, that he could in every other case rely on it as well as he could on that of the hon. member for South Perth.
Mount Forest public building, $18,000.

The tenders for this building have been called for, to be received on the 30th of this month. The site has been bought, having a frontage of 60 feet on Main street, by a depth of 100 feet on Wellington street. The object is to provide accommodation for post office and customs purposes, also armoury accommodation for E company of the 30th regiment, Wellington Rifles. The estimated cost of the building is $25,000. The postal revenues last year amounted to $4,924.33, the money orders issued were $20,113, and money orders paid $26,516. The population by the census of 1901 was 2,019.
What was the cost of the site?

$3,600. It will take about $25,000 in addition Jo the cost of the site to complete the building.
Some resolutions reported.
